subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INTRODUCTION OF MORE APPROPRIATE MEASURE TO DEAL WITH UNOFFICIAL DISCLOSURE OF GOVERNMENT DOCUMENTS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a motion to make under this Standing Order. The urgent and pressing necessity and circumstances are quite apparent from the facts. Whereas an historical analysis of the Official Secrets Act makes it quite clear this legislation was originally passed to deal with espionage and was never intended as a means of punishment to be used by those in authority who might have suffered bruised egoes, embarrassment or red faces through the publication of classified papers in connection with domestic matters, this House requests the government to forthwith review the Official Secrets Act, and in particular Section 4, and propose to Parliament more appropriate measures to deal with unofficial disclosure of such government documents taking into account the principle enunciated at the Nuremburg trials, as well as the overriding need for more open government.

CONDEMNATION OF USE OF PRIVATE INVESTIGATORS BY POLITICAL PARTIES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask the unanimous consent of the House to deal with a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In view of recent disclosures that both major Canadian political parties, the ruling Liberals and the official opposition Tories, have engaged an international intelligence agency for the purpose of monitoring the activities of members of other political parties and in view of the fact that the intelligence agency in question, Inter-tel, Inc., has numerous ties to the United States intelligence community, many of their operators and directors being former employees of the CIA, the FBI or the national security agency, and in view of the fact that it is clear any information gathered through this agency would be available to the United States Government intelligence community thus making a complete mockery of any idea of Canadian sovereignty, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes):
That this House condemn the use by any political party of private investigative firms for the purpose of monitoring political opponents or any government activities and that it especially condemn the use of a foreign intelligence agency which is clearly a free enterprise wing of the secret service agencies of a foreign country.

speechtext:

Considering that, since the adoption of the omnibus bill in 1969, homosexuals, not satisfied with being able to do what they want in privacy, between consenting adults, demand the right to attack children, as evidenced by their manifesto demanding the abolition of all legislation on the age of content, considering also that these repulsive demands clearly show that the liberalization of legislation concerning homosexuality was a mistake, because of the lack of respect shown by homosexuals for the great majority of Canadians, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte):
That the House direct the government to amend the Criminal Code to include a provision making it an indictable offence for an individual to expose publicly his or her homosexuality and to advertise in favour of homosexuality.

subsubtopic: CONCERNING LABOUR'S PARTICIPATION IN GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Labour. In view of the fact that the minister has stressed the importance of a tripartite approach to the solution of industrial strife in Canada through the Canada Labour Relations Council and, keeping in mind that the latest International Labour Organization figures for 1974 show Canada leading all other countries in man-days lost in strikes-that figure of 9.25 million man-days was exceeded last year, and is now 10.5 million-will the minister today clarify the confusion he has created by his statement on May 4 that labour's withdrawal from the tripartite discussions is hopefully temporary and by the equally confusing replies on Tuesday, May 11, when he said that labour's withdrawal paves the way for its participation later?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Labour):
subsubtopic: CONCERNING LABOUR'S PARTICIPATION IN GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not see anything contradictory about it at all.

subsubtopic: CONCERNING LABOUR'S PARTICIPATION IN GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: CONCERNING LABOUR'S PARTICIPATION IN GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext: The fact of the matter is that it is my hope, and I assume the hope of the hon. member, that labour's withdrawal temporary, and the fact that it is a withdrawal rather than a resignation would pave the way for its re-entry later.

subtopic: MEASURES TO SECURE CO-OPERATION OF LABOUR AND REPLACE TRIPARTITE APPROACH
MEASURES TO SECURE CO-OPERATION OF LABOUR AND REPLACE TRIPARTITE APPROACH
speechtext:
It is obvious that the minister does not see any contradiction in his words. In the anti-inflation white paper of October it is stated, and I quote:
There are several structural problems which need to be addressed in a comprehensive anti-inflation program. The third relates to the need to improve labour management relations.
... in co-operation with the two groups directly involved-labour and management-the government will seek practical solutions. The government has established the tripartite Canada Labour Relations Council to assist in this effort.
Oral Questions
This was government policy in October. The Canada Labour Relations Council, for all practical purposes, is now defunct.
I ask the minister, what new policy does he have to replace the now unworkable tripartite approach, and what exactly is the minister going to do to get labour co-operation between now and at the end of controls in December, 1978?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: MEASURES TO SECURE CO-OPERATION OF LABOUR AND REPLACE TRIPARTITE APPROACH
speechtext:
As I have repeated to the hon. member on several occasions, much has been accomplished under the tripartite arrangement. Some initiatives can now be proceeded with, since we were successful in arriving at a consensus and getting agreement from all sides. So the government can now proceed with several of the initiatives in that agreement, and I would be pleased to elaborate on those to the hon. member if he wishes.
Our relationship as a government with labour was never entirely dependent on the tripartite council to which the hon. member referred. The Prime Minister and other members of the cabinet have had many discussions, and other ministers in the cabinet are dealing with labour on an ongoing basis with respect to programs in their departments. I myself am dealing with the leadership of the labour movement in bilateral discussions constantly, and these meetings will carry on.

subtopic: MEASURES TO SECURE CO-OPERATION OF LABOUR AND REPLACE TRIPARTITE APPROACH
speechtext: The minister apparently is saying that officially there is a breakdown, but unofficially there are talks. Does this mean that the minister is actually saying that there is a real possibility that no solutions will be found for better industrial relations for the remainder of the controls program, which would be a loss of nearly three years in this vital area of concern? If this is the minister's dilemma, I invite him to be frank with the House and say so.

subtopic: MEASURES TO SECURE CO-OPERATION OF LABOUR AND REPLACE TRIPARTITE APPROACH
speechtext: Of course it is not. I think a great deal has been accomplished already with respect to initiatives and broader-based bargaining with the desirability in the agreement to have a common data gathering agency which can make findings which will not be suspected of bias by either side. These are some of the things which have been accomplished. I am hopeful that other things will be accomplished with respect to having government involvement with labour, and in addition, labour's input with respect to policies in the post controls period. However, they may not be accomplished under the aegis of the tripartite council, but under some other format in terms of discussions. That is all.

subtopic: EFFECT OF WITHDRAWAL OF LABOUR FROM LABOUR RELATIONS COUNCIL ON DISCUSSIONS CONCERNING POST-CONTROL PERIOD
EFFECT OF WITHDRAWAL OF LABOUR FROM LABOUR RELATIONS COUNCIL ON DISCUSSIONS CONCERNING POST-CONTROL PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the minister. The government has said that the CLC agreed to have discussions with the cabinet with regard to the economy in the post-controls period, reportedly decided at a meeting between the Prime Minister and high union officials in March. Has the withdrawal of the the CLC from the Canada Labour Relations

May 13, 1976
Oral Questions
Council negated the CLC commitment to such talks on the post-controls period as an official body?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: EFFECT OF WITHDRAWAL OF LABOUR FROM LABOUR RELATIONS COUNCIL ON DISCUSSIONS CONCERNING POST-CONTROL PERIOD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not believe so at all. I think the position of the CLC, as the House well knows was that, although the government disagrees and I disagree, it feels that the present selective wage and price control programs is a negation of collective bargaining. Since the tripartite council terms of reference deal almost exclusively with improvements in collective bargaining they did not think they could sit on that body. They have always indicated their desire to meet with the government to discuss policies that would be in their best interests and the interests of the Canadian people in a post-control period. That is why they are willing to participate in these discussions.

subtopic: MEETINGS WITH LABOUR CONCERNING POST-CONTROL PERIOD
MEETINGS WITH LABOUR CONCERNING POST-CONTROL PERIOD
speechtext: A supplementary question. I gather from the minister that there is no official contact with the CLC regarding this post-control period. Could the minister confirm whether similar talks are scheduled with other labour bodies on the post-control problem and, if so, when will they be held, in view of the special committee on post-control policy established by cabinet which wants to promote tripartite business, labour and government talks on economic efficiency and productivity.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: MEETINGS WITH LABOUR CONCERNING POST-CONTROL PERIOD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe the hon. member's original premise is not correct. I think that an agreement has been pretty well reached, subject to confirmation as to the particular day. There will be meetings between the CLC and the government with reference to post control and the general economic attitude of the government some time in June probably. As I said, however, the precise date has yet to be confirmed.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he has read the statement reported to have been made by the United States ambassador to Canada in which he said that a major irritant between our two countries was the lack of adequate defence spending by Canada? subsubtopic: ALLEGED STATEMENT BY UNITED STATES AMBASSADOR CONCERNING DEFENCE SPENDING BY CANADA- GOVERNMENT POSITION

subsubtopic: ALLEGED STATEMENT BY UNITED STATES AMBASSADOR CONCERNING DEFENCE SPENDING BY CANADA- GOVERNMENT POSITION

speechtext: A supplementary, Mr. Speaker. No doubt the ambassador has every right to express his own views. subsubtopic: ALLEGED STATEMENT BY UNITED STATES AMBASSADOR CONCERNING DEFENCE SPENDING BY CANADA- GOVERNMENT POSITION

subsubtopic: INQUIRY IF FEDERAL FUNDS AVAILABLE FOR SENIOR CITIZENS' APARTMENTS IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs.
Is the minister in a position to inform the House whether, recently or a few months ago, any sums of money coming out of the equalization fund or from other sources have been transferred to the Quebec government, and in particular to the Quebec Housing Corporation, for the purpose of building low cost housing for senior citizens? speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: INQUIRY IF FEDERAL FUNDS AVAILABLE FOR SENIOR CITIZENS' APARTMENTS IN QUEBEC

Funds were made available for those programs. I would be happy to discuss that with the hon. member. I do not carry the precise figures for each program for each province in my head. Funds are available for senior citizen housing programs in Quebec.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY IF FEDERAL FUNDS AVAILABLE FOR SENIOR CITIZENS' APARTMENTS IN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question.
Is the minister aware that officials of the Quebec Housing Corporation reply to citizens asking for funds to build low cost housing for senior citizens that they have not received any money and have not had any discussion with the federal government and that, consequently, any
May 13, 1976

application from municipalities or nonprofit private companies gets the same answer that there is no money available? Is the minister aware of that and could he make a statement to clarify the federal government's participation, and where does the matter stand now?

subsubtopic: COMMENTS OF UNITED STATES AMBASSADOR ON CANADA'S DEFENCE SPENDING-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps the House will grant me indulgence for a moment and allow me to extend compliments to General W. W. subsubtopic: COMMENTS OF UNITED STATES AMBASSADOR ON CANADA'S DEFENCE SPENDING-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Now I come to the less satisfactory part of my intervention. My question, directed to the Minister of National Defence, is allied to the question asked by the hon. member for Greenwood; only I direct it to the Minister of National Defence as he has greater responsibility, I believe, for the inadequacies of our defences.
In a speech to a Canadian-American relations seminar in Winnipeg, U.S. Ambassador Enders said a satisfactory level of Canadian military spending is critical to the defence of North America because the U.S. is close to the margin point when it comes to maintaining an effective defence over Europe and North America. He also said that one of the major irritants in Canada-U.S. relations has developed because many Americans believe Canada gives too low a priority to defence spending. Would the minister care to comment on Ambassador Enders' assessment of the contribution which Canada has been making to the defence of the Alliance and also say something about what our future commitments should be?

subtopic: REASON FOR PROPOSAL TO CLOSE BASES
REASON FOR PROPOSAL TO CLOSE BASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question had to do with what the future commitments should be for Canada. I agree that the minister has, in another area, discussed our capital spending increases. They are impressing. Although we have been promised everything, new tanks, fighters and ships, we still have nothing in hand. The promises are not far-fetched, but implementation is certainly far distant.
My question is this: As the government has suddenly seen the error of its ways and now given priority to revitalizing and re-equipping our forces, why is the Department of National Defence proposing to close as many as nine bases, nearly one third of our total?

subtopic: REASON FOR PROPOSAL TO CLOSE BASES
speechtext: But not Calgary.

speakeroldname: Hon. James Richardson (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: REASON FOR PROPOSAL TO CLOSE BASES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the department is not planning to close nine bases.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: REASON FOR PROPOSAL TO CLOSE BASES

subtopic: REASON FOR PROPOSAL TO CLOSE BASES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the figure the hon. member used I believe comes from a statement made by the deputy minister before the parliamentary committee, in which he indicated the difference between the number of bases that were required and the total we have at present. He also made it clear that there was no recommendation coming forward from the department or from me to the government to close nine bases.

subtopic: REASON FOR PROPOSAL TO CLOSE BASES
speechtext: I would like to correct the minister. He has, unwittingly I am sure, misled the House as to what the official said at the defence committee last Thursday. He said that for an effective infrastructure, the department needed only 23 bases whereas they now have 32. Therefore, I assumed that in the infrastructure rationalization paper they must have proposed closing nine bases. If this is not correct, that 32 less 23 equals nine, I would appreciate the minister correcting me and telling me what bases he proposes to close.

subtopic: REASON FOR PROPOSAL TO CLOSE BASES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has just requoted what I said a moment ago. The deputy minister did give those figures. However, he also very clearly said that there were no recommendations before cabinet at this time to close nine bases and that is a fact.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
maintopic: REASON GENERAL DARE SENT LETTER TO COLONEL BOURNE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, surely there are two very simple answers to that. The first is that the letter, as I just said, went beyond what the committee decided and General Dare was using the letter to draw a conclusion and suggesting that it be discussed by officials to see if his conclusion was right. So he was putting that in writing because he wanted to go beyond the cabinet decision and know if he was making a proper inference. In other words, it does happen that cabinet decisions are recorded and they are sent back for supplementary explanations.
The second reason is that in our system of cabinet all cabinet decisions are recorded. We record them for the purpose of the secretariat. I suppose it is acceptable practice that in departments they also put this on record in order to have action further from the record of decision. It seems to me it does not demand very great insight to ask oneself why this was put into a letter. There are two good reasons for that.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a point of order to raise in connection with a matter which in recent years has not been raised too often in this House but which was raised a good many times in prior years. It concerns the privileges of all members of the House in connection with the making of alterations in Hansard. As I understand it, sir, the only alterations any member or cabinet minister is permitted to make to Hansard have to do with punctuation, grammatical errors or spelling errors, and the like, but in no instances are members or cabinet ministers permitted to make alterations to Hansard which change the sense of what was said and recorded by the Hansard reporter in this House. Yesterday, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), and I am quoting from photostat copies of the blues, had this to say:

The blues were altered so that the words "might have" were struck out by the Solicitor General, or his executive assistant or whoever looks after these matters, and the word "had" was substituted for the two words "might have". The record for yesterday, at page 13441 of Hansard, indicates that the words "might have" were restored to the official record, but in the meantime the press gallery had the altered "greens", and indeed in at least one newspaper report this morning the quote of the Solicitor General came out as "I raised the point, which they thought might have been counter productive, that the letter had been destroyed". So now we know that members * of the press gallery do get the altered "blues" in the form of "greens" and that that quote went out over the news media last night in the altered form. Yet today we are confronted with the original form as recorded by the Hansard reporter, and indeed which I heard, in reply to the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton.
Of course, the use of the past tense "had" would completely negate any need for issuing a search warrant to find the missing letter that had been destroyed, so the logic of changing it back to the original future tense becomes very apparent. But even then it does not explain the actions of the Solicitor General. The point is that the complete sense of the Solicitor General's reply to the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton had been altered and then realtered back again so that the form of the record appears accurate, but throughout the country the press used the altered form.
There is another alteration on page L-9 of the "blues", in the third line from the bottom in the Solicitor General's answer, again to the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, where he said, and I go back to the fourth line from the bottom:
-but to get the exact copy that was sent to the Toronto Sun so that we could get evidence as to whether it was produced, how it was produced and who might have sent it.
The word "whether", as recorded by the Hansard reporter, was altered by the Solicitor General to "where", thus completely altering the sense of his answer. It is not a spelling error, a punctuation or grammatical error. That kind of alternation is not an alteration permitted under the rules of the House, because it is a substantive change. Perhaps an alteration might be made by executive assistants, acting on behalf of cabinet ministers, who alter the "blues" to the extent of substituting the past tense for the future tense in the words "might have" with the word "had", and perhaps that might be in order because it certainly gives the wrong indication to the media, which has the power and, in fact, did disseminate this wrong information in its report of events in this place yesterday.

If, as the hon. member for Yukon says, changes were made that appear in the "blues", or "greens" that go to the press gallery, may I say that in my experience those are editorial corrections that the Hansard reporters make when they check back on their notes. When we make any corrections on the white sheets, that does not get photocopied.
I suggest that to accuse the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) of having made any change which appears on the sheets that go to the press gallery is to make an accusation without proof to back it up. The very fact that in the printed version of Hansard it is put back to what was taken down in the first place suggests, to my way of thinking, that there was no alteration on the part of the Solicitor General. He has not asked me to defend him, but one should not be accused unless there is some evidence.

May 13, 1976
Science Policy

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext:
That this House recognizes the necessity of Canada enhancing its scientific and technology efforts for its long-term benefit, and condemns the government for its failure to develop a strong science policy and for not adopting measures that will increase research and development in both the industrial and academic communities.
He said: Mr. Speaker, our motion today expresses not only our view of the state of science and technology in Canada, but I believe it expresses, as well, the view of a large majority of people in Canada in business and in the scientific and academic communities. I believe we could go so far as to say that most people in the department would probably agree with the temper of the motion. About a year ago, the subject of science and technology was debated on an opposition day; to be precise, on June 9, 1975. A review of that debate shows there was general agreement in parliament that increases were necessary for research and development in the sciences and in technology. One only needs to look at the trade figures for 1975. We had an $8.2 billion deficit in high technology trade. That, alone, should cause the government to review its objectives and goals in this area.
A short review of the attitudes of key departments of government shows a lack of purpose and direction. The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Drury) is a part-time minister. I do not say that in a derogatory way; I realize he carries two portfolios and that is an onerous task. He spends three or four hours a week, I understand, on the affairs of the department. He may wish to correct that figure, but that is the information I have. As I read his current view, Mr. Speaker, it is that we have a branch plant economy and perhaps we should purchase our technology offshore. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) echoes the view of the Economic Council of Canada that the future of Canadian industry lies in the development of knowledge-intensive, high-technology industries. These two views seem to be opposed.
Then we have the "on again, off again" special capital cost allowances-short-term in the main-of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), and the Anti-Inflation Board regulations that classify research and development in the same grouping as donations to charity, sales promotion and advertising. The amount spent on research and development by a company is tied to a formula based on previous expenditures. If a businessman wants to increase his research and development expenditures, he must decrease in some proportion his donations to charity or expenditures on sales promotion and advertising. An analysis of those three positions will show the state which science and technology are in from the point of view of the department, from the point of view of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, and from the point of view of the Minister of Finance.

The Anti-Inflation Board regulation will hold back our advancement in industrial technology for years. This policy has resulted in a further withdrawal from industrial research in Canada. Several companies were involved in rather extensive research and development, but they have either moved offshore or to a better financial and unrestricted climate to carry out their work.
We have a welfare state in Canada financed by a resource-based economy. Due to the attitudes and the performance of the Minister of Science and Technology, we will never move out of this trench. In spite of the advice from the Economic Council of Canada and the views put forth by the academic community and the National Research Council, in spite of the views of parliament, and industry, we appear still to fumble and stumble along with the cosmetic policies and platitudes in the minister's speeches about the advances we have made in our short history. We have little time for those who like to state and restate our past achievements about how we set up a department of science and technology. I will always give credit to those dedicated people whose persistence and foresight kept our scientists together over the years.
The problems facing us today are too urgent to allow us to bask in the sunshine of history. There is too much time spent rearranging, not necessarily in chronological order, a series of developments and laying beside it a so-called science policy and then saying our achievements are a result of that science policy. That is a clever psychological trick. How many people involved in administering the research and development programs put forward by the government have worked in the field of science and industrial research. It seems to me they spend more time producing press releases and multicoloured annual reports than looking to the advancement of our scientific knowledge and the translation of that knowledge into technology so that human and economic gains may accrue to the people of Canada and the world at large.
This party believes that scientific research should be financed by government. We believe that the crises we are facing in resources, energy, trade deficits and human wellbeing can only be dealt with by increasing funding for scientific research. We believe the present policies of the government will relegate Canada to the position of a third-class or fourth-class developed nation. We believe the present policies of the government will keep us in the backwater of developed nations and will widen the gap between the rich and the poor in this country. If we continue on our present course, our standard of living will gradually decline and the status of science, education, health and technology will descend to such a level that no amount of money will reverse the trend.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, let me now examine how scientific advancement is accomplished. Money alone is not the answer. The minister has stated this, and I agree with him. It is part of the solution, however, for researchers must be paid, equipment must be purchased and accommodation must be provided. A prime concern must be the environment in which the scientific community works. Scientific excellence cannot be achieved in an environment threatened each year by budget cutbacks and uncontrolled inflation. Scientific budgets have been vastly affected by inflation. Everybody knows this, but there does not seem
May 13, 1976

to be any response to it from the department. The rising cost of equipment has meant a decrease in the number of researchers in a given field. Many post-doctoral researchers are living on a pittance because the project head must try to balance people, budgets and inflation and the purchase of expensive equipment required for his particular field of research.
Scientific achievement is the result of hard work, a gradual building of knowledge in a field of science until, through the efforts of dedicated people, the result being sought becomes evident. That result must be translated into technology, and finally into the gross national product or into the enhancement of the health, well-being and standard of living of the people of Canada and the world. We often read of scientific breakthroughs. That is a journalistic term, Mr. Speaker. I do not really believe there are any scientific breakthroughs. Whatever we achieve in the advancement of scientific knowledge is the result of damned hard work. Our responsibility, as legislators, is to attain an environment stated in firm policy and backed by financial resources to allow the scientific community to pursue their research and to move Canada into the forefront of developed nations.
Great speeches are made by members of the government who say we must help the third world countries, that we must transfer technology to the developing nations, that we must help them advance and improve the quality of life of their citizens. What technology are we going to transfer? What technology will we transfer in the future? Are we going to transfer the branch plant technology the Minister of Science and Technology talks about? Are we going to transfer the knowledge-intensive, high technology the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce talks about? Surely anyone with an ounce of logic must realize that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is really jawboning, as are other people who speak for CIDA when they advance this platitude.
If we do not move on an emergency basis to fund scientific research and research and development in industry, we shall have no technology to transfer to third world nations as we go down the road in the future. If we continue to let our trade deteriorate and our high technology trade balance deficit to increase, we shall place the people of Canada in a precarious position from which they may never recover. If we do not listen to the advice of the Science Council of Canada, the National Research Council, the Medical Research Council, the Economic Council of Canada and the voice of industry, and translate that advice into policy programs which are adequately funded, what future is in store for us? We shall become a second or third-rate scientific community unless we change the attitude of the government.
We must admit what most of us recognize, that a communications gap has opened between legislators and the scientific community. This was ably alluded to by the Science Council of Canada. Organizations such as Scie-Tech and the special committee on science policy in the other place, chaired by Senator Lamontagne, have been helpful and useful in bridging this gap. But the recommendations of the Special Committee on Science Policy have been basically ignored by the government. Instead, we
Science Policy
hear about a balanced policy of scientific research and industrial development as proposed by the Minister.
The people of Canada have the right to know the government's position on the future of this ministry. Will the government continue to downgrade the department, a downgrading made evident by lack of direction and funding? Are we to have a part-time minister in future? Or are we now seeing the demise of the ministry? We went from a full-time minister in 1971 to a half-time minister in 1974. Now we have the part-time minister of today. It would appear that the present minister has been given the task of overseeing the demise of the ministry of science and technology. That is the opinion of many to whom I have spoken in the last few weeks. When the minister was first appointed to this portfolio, people speculated that now we had some muscle in the cabinet. After all, the former president of the treasury board is responsible for overseeing science and technology. That is what people thought.
What is the reality of the situation? I submit that our science policy is heading for disaster. Years of excellent research are being undone, and the advice of the special committee on science policy is ignored. Many research teams are now being disbanded. I have, personnally, seen letters sent to some of our most expert researchers, inviting them to leave Canada and undertake projects in other jurisdictions. Is it not sad that I must report this to the House? If we had half the purchase price of one Orion aircraft, which each cost $60 million, devoted to the advancement of scientific research and the development of industrial technology, we would be in a position to reverse the dangerous course we presently pursue.
In an era of restraint, talk of increasing expenditures brings the usual response from the treasury bench, "They accuse us of talking about restraint but continue to recommend expenditures." When ministers talk in this vein, they are hunting for headlines. They try to discredit any positive recommendation with the use of such tactics. I recall, at the time of the last debate one year ago, going up in the elevator with the minister. He conveyed that very thought to me, saying, "You are talking out of both sides of your mouth. You cannot have it both ways." I say that the government's priorities are wrong. They are out of phase.
The restraint program the government has implemented is, in my view, a dishonest effort at best. There is little or no co-ordination between the ministry of science and technology, the ministry of trade and commerce, and the ministry of finance. One wonders what they talk about if, indeed, they talk. We pour out millions of dollars in low-interest loans or no-interest loans to developing nations. Perhaps we should divert some of that money to science and technology so that in future aid will be available. By doing that we shall make sure that our economy is sufficiently buoyant to aid developing nations and any technology we shall transfer to them in future will be of such a calibre that it will enable developing nations more readily to take their place in the world community.
At a time when there is great speculation about the resources of the world, when gloomy predictions are made about limitations on growth, and when there is talk of more cartels in commodities and resources, the government of Canada appears to be in full retreat. We have in Canada great expertise in earth sciences. There have been major

May 13, 1976
Science Policy
developments in earth sciences in the last decade. We should use that expertise to understand better our resources and utilize better our technology.
I recall that a couple of years ago the members of the House were most interested in the people in western, northern and eastern Canada who were drilling for oil. We debated the subject and asked many questions in the House. Members on both sides spoke in glowing terms of the approximately 100,000 people engaged in drilling for oil and gas, people who rank among the world's most knowledgeable and expert in the field. What has happened to them? You will now find these people all over the world, the reason being our ill-conceived policies on energy and poorly thought-out policies on taxation. Now the government is beating its breast about increased exploration and drilling activities and creating more tax revenue, all in the name of energy self-sufficiency. If the government had possessed the foresight to meld the scientific expertise developed in earth sciences with the expertise of experienced seismic and drilling crews, perhaps we should not be in our present energy difficulties.
Let me turn for a moment to the subject of nationalism. Any time we talk about the academic community, the subject of nationalism seems to raise its head. It is true to say, I think, that in the late 1950s and early 1960s there was a wave of confidence in science. There was a feeling that we could translate much of the research being done into technology and lessen our dependence on foreign technology. With the growth of inflation and a series of cutbacks in research funding in the early 1970s, the hope of developing high technology for a strong, secondary industrial base faded.
We have seen lately an attack on the national origins of some of the leading researchers in Canada. This came about, I submit, because our universities geared themselves to the funding of the federal government and responded to the expansion of universities brought about by the provinces to meet the post-war baby boom. There developed in some fields of research, not necessarily scientific research, a surplus of researchers. It became the vogue to point to the national origin of a particular department head, and if he was not Canadian he was open to criticism. Let me say this: If we ever reach the point at which we assign a nationality to knowledge, expertise, vision and dedication, we shall deal a death blow to scientific research, a blow far greater than such research was dealt by cutbacks in research funding. Not only must we retain our best researchers in Canada but we must, with increased funding, continue to seek out the best minds in the world. I am afraid we shall lose many of our best researchers unless we can pry loose initial funds.
I think the government began its romance with science in the 1960s. In 1971 it appointed the first minister of science and technology. It was felt that the portfolio ought to be a low-profile one. After the initial splash of publicity was over, the first minister in the portfolio adopted a low profile. In fact, I do not think he is very high-profile at any time, in any portfolio. However, that is getting personal and perhaps I should not say that.

The second minister did not really have time to settle into the department before there was another shuffle that produced the present minister. Just in case some members think I am being unduly harsh on the present minister, let me say that I have the greatest respect for that gentleman. He has served Canada in many capacities and in many fields. I say that he has served Canada well.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext:
I have a high personal regard for him. Having said that, I have to question very seriously whether this should be a low-profile ministry. When I see the confusion in the departments of energy, industry and finance, I think that science and technology should not be a low-profile portfolio. I recognize that it is difficult to place achievements in science beside dollars allocated for funding, but that is the nature of science. It is a series of building blocks that are put in place, with the assistance of funding, until a structure is built that produces the result sought when the project was begun. One of the side benefits of scientific research is the spin-off effect from one project into another. It is something that cannot be predicted; it just happens.
Many people have said to me that if Best and Banting were to apply today for funding for insulin research, they would probably be turned down because the criteria have been changed. They would be turned down because of the criteria put forth by this government. There are many other aspects and benefits from the spin-off that are not apparent to us and may not be apparent at the start of a research project.
We are faced today with declining productivity in our industry. I do not know how many people realize it, but last year we lost 11 million man-years due to strikes. We lost more than 11 million man-years in industry last year due to alcoholism and drug use. Surely we must address ourselves to this problem if we are to increase our productivity. We can have the most productive and highly developed technology available, but if it will not overcome the more than 22 million man-hours lost because of strikes, alcoholism and drugs, it is not going to be of much use. I believe we have many serious problems facing us at present, in the future, and as far ahead as we can see. We in this party believe we should have in the House of Commons a standing committee on science and technology.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
I see the hon. member opposite applauding. I believe that his position is the same. We believe it should be, and can be, non-political in its make-up if its terms of reference are properly stated. We believe this could be a means of bridging the gap between the academic and industrial community and legislators. We believe this committee should have input from provincial governments, that it should meet with industrial and scientific groups and should co-operate fully with the committee in the other place. In fact, it may be that we should have a joint committee. Be that as it may, being a House of Commons man, I would rather see a committee here that would
May 13, 1976

co-operate with a committee there, and we could work together on projects.
We believe we should fund scientific research through various departments, on a priority basis. The funding should be projected for a minimum of five years but should be structured on a continuous ten-year cycle. While some scientific researchers do not like direction in their research projects, they must of necessity work toward broad national objectives. Surely, the fields of medical research, energy, ocean sciences, transportation, communications, housing, agriculture and pollution are of national concern. We must harness the scientific expertise we have in these fields and fund them on a priority basis over the next decade.
I cannot accept the philosophy that perhaps we should purchase our industrial technology offshore. That would place us in second or third place forever. While there is much technology we can use that has been developed elsewhere and may be a stopgap solution in the short-term, our long-term objective must be to translate the results of our scientific research into technology that we can use domestically and sell or transfer to others. In other words we must translate it into gross national product. We have to be hardnosed about where we are going. We can only do this if we plan on a continuous ten-year cycle and state the level of our funding on a five-year budget. If we could reach this objective, those involved in the field of research would be able to see where they were going. They would know what funds would be available to them and could time their projects accordingly.
When the minister spoke on June 9, 1975, he said, among other things, and I quote from page 6562 of Hansard:
Put simply, we want to achieve a balanced development of knowledge and research capability in all fields of science and technology. For this reason we propose introducing a more unified and co-ordinated granting structure. The change will not detract from the influence or prestige of either the NRC or the Canada Council. We look to the former to have a major influence in the development of our industrial technological base as well as research into problems which, because of the scale of facilities required or because of time frames, are inappropriate for non-governmental bodies.
Where is the more unified and co-ordinated granting structure? All we have seen is a drastic cutback in all research and a restriction in industrial research and development through regulation of the Anti-Inflation Board. Further in his remarks, the minister stated, again at page 6562, and I quote:
There is no decline in Canada's scientific and technological effort. The emphasis is shifting, I hope, toward growth in the application of science rather than the acquisition of knowledge, but in total I feel that our science and technology are healthy and ready to aid us in meeting the future. If we have a problem in relation to science it is in deciding where to put our money.
Well, they obviously decided not to put the money into science and technology. Because of the cutbacks, they decided not to adjust the budget of science and technology to account for inflation. When we view the cutbacks in this ministry and the cancellation of several research and development projects in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, we have to question the sincerity of the minister when he made these remarks last year.
I have gone on at some length. I know there are other members who wish to contribute to this debate. I will close by saying that we in this party are very concerned about
Science Policy
the future of science and technology in Canada. Unless we reverse the present trend, we shall lose valuable researchers. I have read letters which many of them received from universities in other jurisdictions, inviting them to continue research outside Canada and quoting the size of the funds available for their work. It is a shame that the body of expertise we have built up in this field should be allowed to dribble away. Once these people have left, it will be very difficult to get them back for the benefit of Canada.
What are our plans for industrial development? I have followed the great debate which has raged in connection with foreign-owned corporations and branch plant economies. Unless we continually fund technological development-

I am sure hon. members will agree that businessmen do not put funds into research and development when they are operating at a loss, or merely breaking even; they do so when their enterprises are operating at a high level of profitability. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada has one of the fastest growing labour forces in the western industrialized world. We have tried to meet the needs of this country, according to a special commission of the OECD, by tremendous expansion of educational facilities from kindergarten to post-graduate level. This country is turning out more highly educated, highly skilled people than ever in its history.
The minister of colleges and universities in Ontario was quoted a week ago as saying that in Ontario alone more than 1,000 people were working to get degrees as doctors of philosophy. Extrapolating this figure across the country, and including those working on masters degrees, I would imagine the total number would be in the neighbourhood of 10,000. Many of these people have been looking forward to the time when they would conclude their difficult and extensive work toward their doctorates-looking forward to finding work which was rewarding both financially and in terms of achievement in Canada whether in our universities, in our research institutions, in industry or government.
9SS68-20

May 13, 1976
Science Policy
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious to me that those expectations are not founded on reality. There is unanimous agreement in the scientific community, in the universities, in government and in private industry that there are not, and will not be, positions available to the people who are graduating, and that in fact we have no science policy. Members opposite will, I am sure, maintain that I am saying these things because I take a very partisan view. I admit to being partisan. Let me, therefore, put on record the views of the Royal Society of Canada as expressed in a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in April, 1976, copies of which were sent to all members of parliament. Allow me to quote a few paragraphs from that statement.
Budget freezes and cutbacks along with inflation have so impoverished research and development in all three sectors-government laboratories, universities and industry-that we are facing the break-up of competent research groups . .. the downgrading of the quality and scope of research, and loss of morale among researchers.
The brief goes on to say:
By 1975, government support for industrial research and development (considered as a fraction of gross national product) had declined to 87 per cent of the fraction of GNP it had in 1969.
In government laboratories, the 1975-76 level of financing was only 83.3 per cent of the level in 1969. "This has not arisen because of the transfer of significant amounts of research and development to industries or to universities. This transfer has not occurred. Instead, the decrease has come about as a result of inadequate budgets."
What did the society say about universities?
The situation in Canadian universities is even worse. In 1975, financing had dropped to 67 per cent of the 1969 level.
The letter goes on to point out:
The government has frozen the 1976-77 budgets of the National Research Council and the Medical Research Council, the two granting agencies which provide most of the funds for scientific research in Canadian universities. This freeze will cause a further decline this year to about 60 per cent of the 1969 level.
Senior civil servants are saying the same thing. The president of the National Research Council was quoted in the Financial Post of January 24, 1976, as follows:
Canada will not be able to hold its own in the international market for new and improved manufactured products in a few years time because of these research cuts ... We in Canada have been losing ground since 1969 in the research and development effort so vital to ensure that Canadian products compete favourably in the overseas technological market.
He goes on to point out that the freezing of the budget has meant cutbacks in all the support services which researchers in government institutes need. The government has cut back, or is in the process of winding up, a whole series of programs which we were told just a few years ago, in 1970, were the most promising method of building up our secondary industries to their full competitive potential. I refer, for example, to programs under the Industrial Research and Incentives Development Act and programs designed to ensure greater industrial productivity. Many other agencies created in this field by various government departments are being phased out as rapidly as possible.
Why is it, with government policies developed in answer to criticisms contained in the report by the Senate committee on science policy headed by Senator Lamontagne, criticisms to the effect that government policy was not meeting

the needs of Canadian people, we now see a winding-down completely or a cutback of these programs? It is not just the academics or the theoretical scientists whom I have already quoted who are saying we are in real trouble. Dr. Keith Downey, director of the oilseed program at the Canadian Agriculture Research Station at Saskatoon, who was awarded half the Royal Bank award of $50,000 which is awarded in science, annually, by the bank, for his work in developing Canada's rapeseed crop, one of the major new agricultural crops we are selling in this country, had this to say:
Canadian investment in scientific research and development is falling far short of the level that other developed nations consider essential to their survival. .. Canada's investment of 1.3 to 1.4 per cent of annual gross national product in research and development is only about half the total spent by Western European nations and Japan.
Furthermore, Canada's research outlays equal just 4 per cent of U.S. efforts and are lower than the targets set in 1972 by Ottawa's special Senate Committee on Science Policy.
This country is in a unique position because of its proximity to the United States and because the people, in the main, speak the same language. It is easy for Canadian scientists to pack up and leave Canada, particularly when the government says, as it is every day and has been saying for the last four or five years, that it does not want them, does not need them and does not have the money to finance the work they are doing. It is easy for them to pack, leave and go to the United States.
Efficient and productive research teams built up over the years in Canada are being destroyed and gutted. When the government and the people of Canada wake up, as they will in a year or two, they will realize that we must begin to give support to scientific research and development, which we have not been giving if this country is to survive, grow and utilize the major portion, if not all, of its potential. We will have to begin to recreate these research teams in government institutions, universities and private industry, those same teams which this government would permit, indeed encourage, to be disrupted at the present time.
It is not as though we did not have the researchers who are capable and want to work. Three months ago I put on the order paper a notice for the production of papers asking for the tabling of correspondence between Canadian researchers, scientists in physics, chemistry, agriculture and medical science and the Prime Minister, the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Drury), the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien), and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). This correspondence had reference to the government's policy of freezing or cutting back on funds for scientific research. The government has not yet agreed to table this correspondence and I have not yet seen it, although I have received dozens of letters from people in these fields-and I make no secret of it-or copies of letters sent to the Prime Minister and various ministers. I do not have the time to deal with many of them, but let me quote from one which went to the Minister of State for Science and Technology from a professor of the department of chemistry at the University of Toronto, dated January 16, 1976. He says, in part:
One has only to examine the budgetary treatment of the National Research Council over the past six years to realize that support of basic
May 13, 1976

science in this country has occupied a very low position in terms of federal government priorities. This council, which plays a crucial role for all Canadian university scientists engaged in fundamental research, has received budgetary increases over the period 1970-75 which have fallen far short of increased costs due to inflation. In a period when the consumer price index increased by well over 50 per cent, the NRC budget received cumulative increases totalling only 5.5 per cent. In the forthcoming budget year (1976-77), when the CPI will probably again increase by more than 10 per cent, the NRC budget will be frozen at the already inadequate 1975-76 level.
I do not have time to read the whole letter, but let me put one additional sentence on the record as it indicates that we have people here who are capable and more than qualified to do the kind of work required. This is what Professor Yates says in part of his letter, talking about the calibre of Canadian scientists:
To name just a few from my own university: Geoffrey Ozin was awarded the Meldola Medal (from the U.K.) given annually to the leading inorganic chemist under 35; similarly John Polanyi was awarded the Marlow Medal (also from the U.K.), a corresponding award to the leading physical chemist; Adrian Brook recently won the Kipping Award of the American Chemical Society, given annually to the leading organosilicon chemist-
I am sure that kind of record can be duplicated by many universities in Canada. This is the situation, as I suggested earlier, the government is cutting back on in its winding up of programs and incentives to private fields. Let me just give two illustrations of the failure of these programs, a failure that we on this side predicted at the time. This government has given millions of dollars in grants and loans to RCA for research work in its laboratories in Montreal. RCA Canada had the largest private research laboratories in Canada. That company has made the decision to decentralize its research facilities. That is its decision, and the Canadian operations will ostensibly report to the United States operating division. In fact, I am told that the Canadian research facilities will virtually disappear. The highly educated, highly trained and highly qualified people who are employed there will be either laid off or transferred to the United States. That is an illustration of one result we have had in this country of this government's programs.
Then we have Northern Telecom which, together with Bell Telephone, set up a subsidiary called Microsystems. Microsystems received $34 million in past years to build microprocessors. These are computers of a silicon base which will be used increasingly in telephones, telecommunications, computers and in television sets-you name it, but they will be using microprocessors.
Northern Telecommunications has decided it can sell a lot more of its production in the United States than in Canada. Therefore, it has been proceeding to buy up companies in the United States which do this kind of work. It has been establishing new companies in the United States and is moving its operation to the United States. It will close down its Canadian operation, an operation in which, as I say, in the last few years we have spent $134 million.
Anything that has been learned as a result of the expenditure of that money which was received from the Canadian government will be used to make profits in the United States and to employ people in the United States. The policy of the government in respect of support for private
Science Policy
industry and for research and development has been, as the Minister of State for Science and Technology admitted, a failure. I would put it more strongly and say it has been a complete failure. It has been a failure because the government, as I said at the beginning, has no science policy and has not thought through what it hopes to do with regard to support for scientific research and development.
The government does not know what products it should try to develop. Therefore, it does not know what sort of research and development it should be funding and what kind of companies have a chance to market the products which might be developed. The government, therefore, does not know what skills it should try to establish and what skills should be taught at the manpower training centres. It does not know what kind of people it should be helping and supporting in their undergraduate studies at Canadian universities. The reason is very basic. The government has no industrial strategy. It has no strategy which will allow it to set research and development priorities over the next number of years. The government should try to sort out how it should fund its hit-and-miss research process which is funded now on an ad hoc basis. Such a strategy is difficult to construct, but this country will be in a great deal of economic and social trouble in the next few decades if we do not really think through what is needed in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly appreciate the tone that the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) injected at the beginning of his comments. Sometime in a motion of this nature we end up arguing and someone trips both of us. However, the member does show a sincere interest in the topic, and honestly seems prepared to make recommendations in which all of us might be interested. I hope, for my part, that I might be able to do the same.
The hon. member for Halton-Wentworth referred to the minister as being very low-profile. I think the minister would agree that probably the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth and myself have more weight, either separately or together. Perhaps that is not a profile. I also notice the hon. member mentioned something about there being something dishonest, basically, in the thought of dealing with industry, trade or finance as though the departments might not really be working with each other but moving in different directions. It seems to me that the minister has had pretty close consultation with the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
We have heard talk of the possibility of there being a super-corporation probably to deal with the air-frame companies in Canada. If this were done, obviously one would presume there would be some research moves in the direction of inventory and manufacturing capabilities in this country today. The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce probably has some close contact with science and technology in this regard.
At the finance end, I would presume the finance department has probably had more contact than anyone else, because although there was a reference to a cutback, I notice in the budget that, rather than being a cutback, there was a 13.6 per cent increase, and in respect of the average department we are dealing with a 13.5 per cent increase. So it appears that science and technology has been dealing with finance.
One of the great problems is the discussion of pure research versus the very practical technology industrial type of research. I must be fair about this. My main interest, being English, is that I speak somewhat as a layman. I leave the really serious scientific side to members who are highly qualified in this field, such as the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Maine) and some members on the other side who I know have strong and good views on this subject. As I say, my main interest is English and I have received the odd gold medal for public speaking, but I would say that the best medal I have received, or the most important, would be the copper medal I received from a football team for common sense.
Perhaps there should be some common sense here, and maybe some ordinary souls should speak out. With a minister as interested and as diligent as the one we have, a minister with as broad a range of interests in science as he has, a minister with a profound interest in art, music and the writings of Khalil Gibran and others, and also a strong interest in science and technology as evidenced by his own
(Mr. Orlikow.]
capabilities and applauded by the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth, I think I can speak to him in a common sense way, and perhaps as a person I might say to him that I make a plea for pure research rather than continually developing the industrial and practical side. It may be that Franklin's wife said, "Hey, Ben, go fly a kite" and we got all these lights. Maybe it was not planned, and maybe he did not have the lab going at that time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext:
I think we have to take note of the fact that we do not know if in some areas of research people are doing a study into the coefficient of the speed of skating in relation to the size of the blade and the size of the rink. This sounds like interesting research, but I assume that when the blades get big enough, they back up against the boards and you stop. I do not know why you should have to reearch that. When the blades get bigger, they slow you down. Other people might do research into basketball rebounding. It is very interesting to stand and throw a ball up and see in which direction it goes-but if you are not in the direction it went, there is not much point in throwing it up in the first place.
I must say that in my opinion the layman has something to say here, and since I have spent some time at universities and I have some friends whom I meet across the country, since I have met people in la belle province at the Universite de Montreal, since I graduated from McGill myself and have spent some time in the maritimes at Mount Allison and, of course, my close connections at McMaster and with the west through UBC and Alberta, this brings me in touch with many people who are concerned at this time.
I consider the motion before us today a very serious one. It deals with a specific area of government activity, but in a broader sense it reflects our total country today. I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak because it affords me the opportunity to respond to the remarks of the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth. I have mentioned his name several times because I really believe he has set a tone which I hope will be maintained through the entire day when we will be putting forward some of our own ideas which we think are of benefit to all concerned.
I have met many great teachers, professors and researchers through these years and I have come to admire their dedication and skill. During the past several months I have met with many, both here in Ottawa, in other parts of the country and at McMaster in Hamilton. In our discussions I have been most impressed with their commitment to Canadian research and their concern for our research capabilities in the future.
At this time, the entire nation and every aspect of it is battling the war against inflation. The inflation rate in Canada has caused hardship on all sections of our society. Research is not exempted. Our dollar does not get us today what it did in the past. Our research dollar does not provide the same benefit today as it did yesterday. This [DOT] situation has unique effects on continuing research in Canada. Those who work in research may feel forced to leave Canadian centres to seek a better environment in which to work and live. Programs which have developed over the past years may suffer and never be completed

because of lack of continued funding. We may lose for years the one cure that we have worked for and to which we are so close.
I have another great fear. At our universities research plays a dual role. It provides for society today, and trains our scientists for tomorrow. A university teacher engaging in original research is able to bring to his teaching of undergraduate and graduate courses a first-hand excitement and freshness in presenting the latest in new scientific knowledge.
There are reasons why we are all concerned about the status of Canadian research. We are one of a few nations with a wealth of resources and a low population density. This will permit the creation of a future society, implementing western ideals and avoiding past errors. We can mould our future on the basis of national analysis and creative imagination. This potential, in itself, is a valued resource. This resource may suffer also. Mr. Speaker, the value of research is not only the good news it brings us, but also its ability to warn us of danger and prepare for these dangers. It is a cost we bear today for tomorrow. There are the concerns that have been presented to me by the research community in Canada. They are concerns for Canada today and for our future.
Mr. Speaker, I have spoken of the ill-effects of our restraint program on research in Canada. I have said this without embarrassment, for I know it was a difficult decision the government took-a decision they would rather have not taken. However, the seriousness of our present economic situation called for strong, firm leadership. The cutbacks demonstrated to all the government's ability to show leadership in difficult times. The word "cutback", do not forget, is not to be confused with the government actually going in and cutting back. The fact is that in these inflationary times the amount available, even with increases, means that those in charge within the research areas would have to make these decisions themselves. They have taken this responsibility and they have made the decisions, but still they indicate to us-and in some ways I hope they will win the battle-that more priority should be given to them and that, as we move toward the end of the control period, some day we should be planning now to give more priority to research than we have in the past so that we do not contribute to what might be called intellectual colonialism where we depend on research coming from elsewhere and holding us in its grasp. We may utilize those fine researchers who come and work in our communities and help develop our young students, but we must also utilize our own young students, doctors and researchers so that we do not become victims of intellectual colonialism.
The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Drury) is well aware of what I have said. In October, 1975, the minister wrote a paper for Science Forum which indicated not only the government's commitment to the science policy in Canada but also a firm understanding of how the scientific community functioned, its problem and its need. I know the minister would welcome all hon. members' views and thoughts on this topic. I have every confidence that all recommendations would be considered with a fairness and freedom which we have come to expect from the minister.
Adjournment Motion
Canadian research has produced good things for Canada and the world. Our medical research has reduced suffering and death. Chemical and industrial research advances have put Canada in an enviable position. Our nuclear research and development is highly acclaimed throughout the world. On a more personal level and a more important one, our children do not die from diphtheria, our contemporaries can live satisfying lives with diabetes. There are many ways in which we benefit from past medical research. Does not our generation have an obligation to leave to our grandchildren the benefits of our contribution to the control of other as yet uncontrolled diseases?
Mr. Speaker, I have spoken of the present hardships facing research in Canada today. I have spoken of the success we, as a nation, have seen in this important area. We should be equally disturbed and proud at this time. I have said that the minister would receive recommendations in good faith and with fairness. I believe that research can only thrive in a climate of continuity. We risk too much if funding is "stop and go". The scientific community seeks to moderate the size of the downswings in funding, and this preoccupies them to advocate forcefully a solution of continuity. We should structure our research activity in such a way that both politician and scientist can work with the economic resources available. We should consider the advantage of more effective and direct communication between scientist and government. Only in this way will the research community and government be able to better serve Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, we in Canada have much to be concerned about. The government has shown leadership in its fight against inflation. We know the program is working. It is important, during this period, that we concern ourselves with the days ahead. I see a strong light at the end of the tunnel, and it gets brighter all the time. While they are hard time, they may also be the best times. The people I have spoken with on the matter of funding for research share this view. It is willingness to work together and to labour in Canada for the good of all Canadians. There is an appreciation of the current situation in our economy. There is a belief in the future, and a conviction that it will be better. We can, indeed, spend and study today to plan for tomorrow.
