The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Kempling:
That this House recognizes the necessity of Canada enhancing its scientific and technological efforts for its long-term benefit, and condemns the government for its failure to develop a strong science policy and for not adopting measures that will increase research and development in both the industrial and academic communities.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I begin my remarks I might just comment on a couple of the items raised by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane). In his assessment of Canada's research, development, scientific and technological efforts, he sees a light at the end of the tunnel. I suggest to the hon. member that if he is going to be accurate in his assessment of our situation in Canada today, that is a headlight of a train coming the other way.
The hon. member made another interesting statement. He indicated that spending on research, development, science and technology by the government would be frozen until the end of the controls period. I hope that was an error in semantics, or an error in language, and not an error in fact with regard to an indication of the intent of the government, because the situation is far from being rosy and far from being a situation which is getting better daily, as might be indicated by the metaphor "the light at the end of the tunnel."
My friend and colleague, the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling), who introduced this motion today, indicated that it was just about one year ago, on June 9, 1975, that I had the honour of introducing a motion on an allotted day dealing with the subject of the Liberal administration's science policy for Canada. That motion not only had the support of all opposition parties, but was also supported to a greater or lesser degree by a number of speakers from the other side of the House.
That day marked the first time in the history of this House of Commons that a full day was allotted to debating science and technology, and by and large the debate was erudite and of a high level. Several hon. members, albeit mainly from the opposition, spoke with supporting facts and figures about Canada's comparatively poor performance in this vital area. Hon. members from all parties, including the minister, acknowledged the importance of science and technology to Canada's and to the world's future. Yet comparing this administration's commitment to support science and technology for last year and this year, there is a deterioration: apparently this administration, when confronted with the issue of science and technology, is prepared to genuflect, but beyond that to do nothing

whatsoever to demonstrate a sincerity of belief in the importance of science and technology to Canada's future.
In this technological age it is fair to say that there are few, if any, aspects of our society which are not affected by science and technology. However, in the context of the issues facing Canada today there are a few areas which are affected more than others by science and technology, toward which a meaningful science policy must be specifically directed. One of the scars remaining on the Canadian economy as a result of the policies of the Trudeau administration is the seriously weakened secondary or manufacturing sector of the economy. To a large degree, industries within this sector can be termed high technology industries. This deterioration has certainly had a bad effect on our trade, but another effect has been to lower the rate of employment in these industries. The current unemployment rate is at a record level, 7.4 per cent, and is directly related to the lack of health and vitality in this very important, high technology sector of our economy-and this the Trudeau government refuses to acknowledge in any substantial way.
In addition to its effect on highly technological industries, science policy is absolutely essential to any positive program of Canadianizing our economy and reducing our dependency on foreign investment, because foreign investment and foreign technology go hand in hand. The issue may have dropped from the front pages, but there are still millions of Canadians who want to see this government take positive steps toward the goal of increasing the proportion of our economy which is owned by Canadians.
To a very large extent the quality and quantity of life of Canadians will depend upon how we utilize science and technology. To even the most myopic observer our scientific potential is nowhere near being matched by our performance. With positive programs and strong initiatives we can effect dramatic improvements in such areas as housing, education health care, food, production, and urban transportation. It is difficult to imagine any aspect of our Canadian economy which is not affected by science and technology, but the problems associated with the above four areas in particular, namely, secondary industries foreign investment, quality of life and the environment, can be cured through the implementation of a meaningful science policy. The present ad hoc approaches of this government are simply unsatisfactory.
The other day, when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) introduced his follow-up or second green paper on energy and analysis of Canada's potential energy policies, he introduced a new term selfreliance, as opposed to self-sufficiency. It was introduced in a context which is desirable for Canada for self-sufficiency in energy. I would go so far as to say it is extremely desirable and necessary that as a national we be self-reliant and that we not rely on other nations for our welfare. It is only through self-reliance that we can have freedom of action to pursue goals which are meaningful to Canadians so that we can have the security which is so necessary for a good life. That is the only way in which we can pursue independent policies which will provide Canadians with the better life they deserve and can have.
However, in talking about self-reliance I think it is necessary to acknowledge that it would be foolhardy to

seek self-reliance and self-sufficiency in all things. Quite clearly, we will never be self-reliant in bananas or pineapples, but one can identify three very key elements of our society in which it is imperative that we be self-reliant if we are going to have true self-reliance as a nation. The first of those areas is, of course, energy. In the last three or four years we have had ample demonstrations of how precarious a nation's future is if it is not self-reliant in energy, and we in Canada have that potential. The second area is food. A country which consumes more food than it produces is in a very precarious position, and one in which we as a country need not be in. Indeed, we are not-and I trust and hope that the government recognizes this. The third leg of this stool which forms the foundation upon which a self-reliant nation can be built is the area of technology. The government apparently does not even recognize the necessity for self-reliance in technology, because if we must continue as we have in the past and as we are today increasingly relying on foreign technology, we will never be able to have the freedom of action to pursue Canadian policies and Canadian goals which we want and deserve.
Self-reliance is not synonymous with isolation or with putting up barriers. A nation can be self-reliant and maintain active trade with the rest of the world, as indeed Canada does; but in order to trade I think it has to be recognized just what commodities a country has to trade. I think this can be broken down into four basic commodities. A country can obviously trade in renewable produce, agricultural goods, wood and wood products or hydroelectricity if it is generated in that form. These products we have in relative abundance, and through them we achieve a favourable trade balance. These items are products from non-renewable resources such as iron, steel, oil, gas nickel and other minerals. Canada produces and exports these in great abundance. It is very much like a farmer who maintains a standard of living by selling off a piece of the farm every year. Eventually the farm is sold off and there is no capital left, so the farmer has no means of making a livelihood. We cannot continue, in perpetuity, to rely on the sale of non-renewable resources to finance our standard of living. We can sell a third commodity, as any nation can-the sweat of the brow of its people. The Canadian people would never tolerate the long working hours and low pay necessary to make us competitive with some third world nations whose main component in the manufacture of commodities is brawn.
This leaves only one alternative, and that is to sell the skill, talent and technology of Canadians. This comes in two parts, the buying and selling of talent and, more important, the sale of technology in the form of value added in the manufacture of high technology products. In this area our performance as a nation is nothing short of disastrous. I have before me the trade figures for the last 25 years, broken down by groups, from Statistics Canada. Until 1970 our trade imbalance in high technology was $2Vi billion. That was not good, but we produced more than enough primary products to pay for our negative balance in high technologies.
Since 1970, two years after the present government assumed office, there has been a steady, straight-line
Science Policy
deterioration in our trade performance in high technology. In 1975 our negative balance in high technology trade was $8,192 million, an astromonic and disastrous figure. If this straight line continues, the nation will soon be bankrupt. We will have to resort to the draconian measures that Great Britain resorted used. There is precious little evidence that the government recognizes the severity of these figures. They certainly do not show that they recognize it by offering tangible programs and policies.
How is all this related to research and development? Coincidentally-possibly coincidentally, although I do not think so-we examine the figures which relate to gross expenditure on research and development as a percentage of the gross national product, and we see that the peak was in 1969. For years prior to this our research and development efforts were increasing as a percentage of the gross national product. In 1969 they represented 1.33 per cent of the gross national product. That is half of what the United States spends on research and development, Mr. Speaker, and it was the second lowest figure amongst industrialized nations in the western world. Since then there has been a steady deterioration closely paralleling the deterioration in our trade balance in high technology goods. In the latest figures I have, for 1974, .84 per cent of the gross national product was spent on research and development-one-third of what is spent by the United States, and that compares badly with industrialized western nations.
It is absurd for hon. members opposite to claim that we have a great minister who knows how important this is and who is working hard on behalf of science and technology in Canada. We have not seen that demonstrated. The minister may have had a fine record in the past, but his recent record is abysmal. This disastrous trend has to be reversed, Mr. Speaker, but the options are limited. We can resort to such draconian measures as Great Britain took, and devalue our dollar, impose high tariffs, put on exchange controls and all those things that are predicted by the pessimists. Already capital is leaving the country in anticipation of such measures because people see that evidently the government has no other programs to offer.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext: Could you name them?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext:
I could, but I will not. If the hon. member does not know about them, that is the typical myopia of members on the other side. They should read the newspapers. Our second alternative is to buy the technology needed in order to compete in the world. But that is self-defeating. A high percentage of our economy is already foreign-owned. Foreign technology does not come without foreign ownership; they go hand in hand. Xerox, Kodak and Polaroid have technology-but no amount of money could buy it. They can all set up branch plants in this country, but of course that does not cure our trade problems. The third and only reasonable alternative is to develop our own technology. Unfortunately, this government has not demonstrated any appreciation of this option.
In my opening remarks I noted that this is the second time that science and technology has been debated in this House-both times, I might note for the record, at the initiative of this party, and that says something about the priority given the matter by the government. In another sense, it has to be recognized that the House of Commons

May 13, 1976
Science Policy
is not the only forum for such a discussion. The question of science policy has been discussed widely outside this House. For example, the Senate Committee on Science Policy, the Lamontagne committee, has been studying Canada's science policy since 1965. It has produced three reports containing a multiplicity of excellent recommendations which have not been implemented. The committee is now hearing witnesses and trying to draw to the attention of the government the disastrous path that has been followed.
The Science Council of Canada, funded by the federal government for the purpose of examining science policy, has been in operation a number of years and has produced excellent reports and materials. The minister, who I guess devotes three or four hours a week to the department, has no time to read the reports. Evidently he has not been briefed by anybody who reads them. There is not one iota of evidence to show that the government has paid the slightest attention to what that scientific group has been saying. Scie-Tech, the Canadian Association of University Teachers, and a multiplicity of technical organizations across the country, have all commented extensively and contributed valuable studies and data on the subject. But judging from how the government has responded-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not prevail on the House much longer. I was of the opinion that our speeches were to be limited to half an hour, not 20 minutes. I will summarize by saying that the Science Council recently submitted a brief to the Special Committee of the Senate on Science Policy indicating the six areas in which in the 1960s our scientific and technological posture was seriously weak. Evidence accompanied the material; it is available to the minister and anybody else interested. It shows that in each of these areas the situation remains precarious and difficult.
In summary, let me spell out quickly the things the government ought to do. Regulation 12 of the Anti-Inflation Board should, as the hon. member for Halton-Went-worth suggested, be changed. That would cost the taxpayer nothing and could stimulate research and development.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext: I agree.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext:
The government could institute positive research and development incentives, because the amount of industrial research and development undertaken in this country is steadily decreasing. There must be more direct government spending in this area. As the previous speaker, the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth indicated, in the present period of restraints the government, unfortunately, can do nothing. But it has decreased spending on research and development since 1970. In periods when government spending rose 28 per cent, 32 per cent and 29 per cent

respectively, spending on research and development went down. Therefore, no person opposite can claim that research spending decreased this year owing to constraints of the restraint program. That, Mr. Speaker, has been this government's posture virtually since it took office. I am convinced that not until this government is turfed out will there be any change in this policy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have some bad news, some good news, and some more bad news. First, I thank the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) for bringing this issue to the fore in the House today. It is an important issue and deserves more attention. I support the hon. member's suggestion regarding the creation of a standing committee of the House of Commons on science and technology.
Now I come to the bad news. I feel that Treasury Board must be condemned for its policy of freezing university and government research budgets, and I include the budgets of the National Research Council, the Medical Research Council and the Social Science Research Council. This policy has done much damage and is doing much damage. It will be hard to tell how much damage this policy will ultimately do. The hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) said he thought the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane) had said that this was to be an ongoing freeze. With respect, that is not how I understood the comments of the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain. I understand it is to be a one-year freeze. At any rate, that is what I understood the hon. member to say. Even so, a one-year freeze is not satisfactory.
Mr. Speaker, our present standard of living is the direct result of the harnessing of science, engineering and technology. This will be true to an even greater extent in future. It is very shortsighted indeed to tinker with our standard of living, which is exactly what the freeze is doing. So far as I can see, this dastardly policy has brought only one benefit. It has aroused the scientific community as it has never before been aroused-and it is about time, too. It is about time the scientific community realized that it, like others in the economy, must explain and justify how they spend the taxpayers' dollars. I urge people in the scientific community to organize, to join organizations like SCITEC where they can make their case known. Let them advise their members of parliament so that we can, within this political process, be informed of the problems of the scientific community. In this way we can also inform them of the realities of politics.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext: Great stuff.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext: Well said.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext:
I feel that Treasury Board has made a mistake. But then, any government, or any person cannot avoid, if action is to be taken, the making of mistakes. Only if you do nothing can you guarantee that no mistakes will be made. The great thing is to minimize your mistakes and to learn from the mistakes you make.
I say that the government is to be commended for establishing the Ministry of State for Science and Technology. In 1971 the government considered a new concept, a difficult concept which had never been put into practice. The ministry was set up, action was taken and mistakes were
May 13, 1976

made. But the government learned from those mistakes. Last summer, three years after being established, the new minister, having been installed in office in 1974 and having learned about the department's problems, action was taken and the department was reorganized. What has emerged is a completely new organization-and new faces with it. You will now see new faces in the entire top structure of the Ministry of State for Science and Technology. In the last nine months the ministry has accomplished more than most departments accomplish in decades.
Initially, MOSST made the mistake of adopting too high a profile. This created difficulties and made it difficult for the department to accomplish what it deemed was necessary. The department was ineffective. That, primarily, is why the reorganized department has adopted a low profile. It wants to be effective, and it is now doing its work without making a lot of noise about it. People who do not understand the department have criticized it for adopting a low profile. But people in the scientific community and those closely associated with the department know why this must be so and give the department full credit for what it is doing.
In this connection, may I quote from issue No. 8 of the proceedings of the Special Committee of the Senate on Science Policy, commonly known as the Lamontagne committee. On Wednesday, March 31, 1976, Mr. John Shepherd, executive director of the Science Council, that advisory body to the government, said, as reported on page 8:15 of the Minutes of Proceedings of that committee:
At a very practical level MOSST is performing exceedingly well now as compared to the way it performed two or three years ago. It is struggling manfully to make the contracting out policy work, for example; it has established very effective relations with many mission departments: it is being extremely co-operative in science policy problems such as the transfer of technology from government laboratories to industry; and there is every indication that at that level of practical, low profile co-operation, MOSST is indeed performing very much better than it has hitherto.
The brief of the Science Council is printed as an appendix to that same issue of the committee proceedings. Paragraph 55 of the brief states:
As an agency of the federal government, MOSST needs to respond to immediate problems and thus is oriented to short and medium-term issues. In addressing these problems, its role is to exercise influence rather than to wield power. In the vernacular, MOSST must have a low but distinctive profile.
Because it is a low profile department does not mean that action has not been taken. The people responsible for this action have been very effective. What has been this reorganization? We have a new secretary who was a deputy minister in the Department of National Health and Welfare. He brings with him the knowledge of the organization of government. Being a deputy minister, he knows how it works. Under the deputy minister we have three assistant secretaries covering government, industry and university. The man heading the government branch is a government man with 20 years experience dealing with different departments of government. He is very smooth, diplomatic and effective. In nine months he has accomplished a tremendous amount in getting that department working smoothly and co-operating with other departments of government with which it has to deal. The uni-
Science Policy
versity branch has as its head an ex-vice-prefeident of the University of Quebec at Three Rivers. She is a very efficient, effective woman, who is extremely well qualified and knows the university sector. I only hope the civil service does not grind down the efficiency which she has displayed to date.
The other sector-the most important one in so far as our economy is concerned-is the industry branch. The industry branch has been doing exactly the things in the last six to nine months that I have been advocating, and that is the primary reason I am in this House today-my concern with science in industry. It is almost an extension of Treasury Board, and as such has been extremely influential in the science policy that has been implemented in so far as the funding of science as every budget has to go through Treasury Board.
In the industry branch there are three primary areas it has been working on that are of extreme importance to this country. Make or buy, a policy whereby we are trying to transfer more technology to Canadian industry had been working very successfully with the assistant secretary of the industry branch when he was in the Department of Supply and Services, the most effective and effecient branch of government I have heard of. They were able, within two or three months from receipt of an application, to have a signed contract out to the applicant. With most departments of government I cannot even get a reply to a letter within two or three months, let alone a signed contract from initial contact. That policy has been in effect for a short period of time, since the first minister introduced it. It is now being re-evaluated to see if it can be improved in any way. Some have worked, some have passed their usefulness and others need a revamping because they have not accomplished all the objectives. An extremely important factor for science in Canada in industry is how to encourage the entrepreneur. How do we harness his talents to benefit the Canadian economy? The government is beginning to understand the importance of

I would like to go into detail on a current problem, one that occurred last month with regard to the RCA labs in Montreal. Radio Corporation of America decided to reorganize its company. The government has to stand up, take notice and do something about this. We cannot carry on this way even though it is a branch plant of the United States. It will be more so in the future.
If you enjoy your standard of living and you want to enjoy it more, you had better not cut off our funding. To treat it as a charity, or an area where we should not increase our spending, is absolutely ridiculous. I appreciate the necessity of the Anti-Inflation Board guidelines to get across the message of restraint in this country. We have to beat inflation. However, you do not cut off your right hand in doing it when it will provide our future. Research and development, science, engineering and technology-that is our future. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to enter this debate. May I say at the outset that I certainly agree with the first part of the observations made by the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Maine). However, I take exception to his description of the Ministry of Science and Technology, and I plan to develop this theme later.
Members who have followed the debate and who have listened to the speeches by the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling), the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), and my hon. friend from Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), will recognize that there is a great deal of diversity of scientific endeavour which touches on the lives of all Canadians. I want to focus on two important points. I want to reassess the Ministry of Science and Technology, to take, as it were, an overview. Then I wish to turn to an area which I believe holds out a great challenge, one to which the government has not addressed itself: it is the development of institutions capable of handling the explosion of knowledge we have witnessed in recent years.
Before going further, I wish to compliment the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth for introducing this motion, one which clearly reflects the government's disregard for the importance of science and its inability to establish a science policy for Canada. After four years of existence, the Ministry of State for Science and Technology is on the verge of collapse and its operations during that period can best be described as ineffectual and powerless. When the ministry was first established it was formulated, one might say, with sex appeal and presented as the government's response to the need for providing better scientific and technical advice to various government departments. This exercise was doomed to failure for three reasons. First, with its limited budget it was obvious the ministry would be unable to generate the expertise necessary if it were to develop a forceful voice for science in government circles. Second, in keeping with Parkinson's law, it was inconceivable that a fledgling ministry could have any significant impact on well-entrenched departments with extensive in-house research expertise available to them. Third, the ministry's mandate was doomed to failure from the outset because it lacked authority for action.
In response to the inevitable failure of the program, the government introduced its new science policy for Canada during the Speech from the Throne in 1974. A kit was circulated providing background information which was interpreted by many as the forerunner of the establishment of a super-ministry. In commenting on the National

May 13, 1976

Research Council, the Medical Research Council and the Canada Council, the document stated:
Generally the councils have been successful in achieving their major objectives. However, the disciplinary approach to financial assistance has not produced sufficient balance among the various research disciplines. Further, the increasing importance of interdisciplinary research demand financial assistance to this field of endeavour.
There is still a need for financial assistance programs on a disciplinary basis. At the same time there is a growing and increasingly urgent need for a stronger co-ordination of the granting councils to assure support of a balanced development of knowledge and research capability.
The science policy enunciated in the Speech from the Throne and accompanying documents envisaged substantial changes which would have far-reaching effects on public policy. The scope and authority of the ministry were to be broadened and strengthened to such an extent as to give it the potential for affecting virtually every scientific endeavour carried out in Canada. The changes proposed were to involve not only government structures but future policy orientation and development. Thousands of the most able and highly qualified people in the country, together with teaching and research institutions across Canada, would be directly affected. With hundreds of millions of dollars at the department's disposal every year, the total spectrum of research and development would be directly related to government priority and national goals. What happened to these grandiose ideas? The minister disappeared. The promises contained in the Speech from the Throne vanished, and the responsibilities of the important portfolio concerned have been relegated to the Minister of Public Works.
The final chapter in the demise of the ministry was written when the present minister announced, in September of last year, that the existing policy would be scrapped and replaced by three branches with responsibility for science policy in the government, university and industrial sectors respectively. As if this were not a sufficient indication of the low priority attached by the government to the development of a science policy, he also stated that a corporate services branch would take over responsibility for the administration of the ministry.
We have now come full circle. Having begun with the expectation that the government would show genuine concern about developing a science policy, we have reached the present position in which we find a minister without authority, without a policy and-what is even worse- without any apparent interest in shaping future government policy in this field.
My own views of the importance of research and development are well known. Work in this field has been a major source of economic growth; it has been responsible particularly for the creation of new industries in the areas of electronics, chemicals and computer technology. The search for improvements in productivity has made it possible to expand output while lowering costs.
It is not my intention this afternoon to attempt to cover the broad spectrum of science programs, neither do I wish to go into detail respecting the low priority the government has attached to science in Canada. To place the subject in perspective, a brief comment on the Medical Research Council will serve to illustrate what has been the experience in other areas of scientific endeavour. In the
Science Policy
relatively short span of eight years, the prestigious Medical Research Council has seen its confidence in the future replaced by financial crisis. Funds for medical research have not kept pace with the demands of society or with the expectations of the research community. In terms of constant dollar value, funding has declined. Increased difficulties have arisen in deciding on which discipline or project money should be spent. Increased difficulties have been encountered in attracting and retaining highly qualified people. There is a growing feeling that the quality of research staff and the significance of their work is not recognized by policy-makers responsible for funding research.
The resulting atmosphere of stagnation has created new phenomena, alien to many in the academic and research community, which will inevitably have an adverse effect on the quality of health care. I find it incomprehensible that the federal government should budget such an infinitesimal sum of money for research into health and welfare, such an important cornerstone of our national health system. For reasons which have never been explained, or perhaps even comprehended, those responsible on the benches opposite have refused to accept the principle that medical research, medical education and the quality of health care are inseparably linked.
In the few remaining minutes I have I wish to comment briefly on the urgent need and, indeed, the challenge confronting the federal government to develop the political capacity and understanding to respond in a very positive way to developments in the scientific community.
Perhaps the most important challenge of our generation has been the immensity of the technological revolution and our inability to develop political institutions and the intellectual capacity to deal effectively with these changes.
We have to recognize there are many thoughtful people, including those in various scientific disciplines, as well as consumers, who are asking the basic question if this technological revolution is producing dehumanization. I do not pretend to have the complete answer to that question, but I believe in part it is related to the difficulties we are experiencing in defining humanism in terms that are universally acceptable and, secondly, the infinitely difficult task of defining the technological revolution in terms that Canadians understand and in a context that will eliminate fear and assure the security and peace of mind Canadians are seeking.
The technological revolution has been characterized by an explosion of knowledge that is advancing at a pace faster than politicians understand, or at least admit that they understand, and what is readily apparent is that the pace of this advance is accelerating year by year. I have no doubt that by the end of this century man will learn more about himself and his environment than he has learned in all the history of recorded time, and yet despite this obvious fact the government has ignored this particular challenge and has remained mute.
Scientific progress and knowledge have produced and will continue to produce a total change in man's economic, social, and moral environment, yet the government has

May 13, 1976
Science Policy
developed Minamata vision and fails to act in response to this challenge.
The danger of this change is not the burden or responsibility of the scientific community, but rather the danger is that we have not seen a corresponding change in our political institutions to deal with this knowledge which may be decisive as to whether the course of change will be for good or for evil. For example, the development of the atomic bomb has created a fundamental change in all our thinking regarding relationships with other nations.
We see a growing concern in the world community regarding the risks of nuclear warfare, yet despite our fears there has been a proliferation in the number of nuclear weapons and a failure of our political institutions to reverse this trend, and an absence of universal moral persuasion to force our politicians to eliminate there weapons. Canada as an intermediary power with the technological know-how should be a leading moral voice in attempting to resolve this issue. Our record, which has been debated very many times in this House of Commons, gives evidence to the contrary.
The disparity between the developed and non-developed nations is a well recognized problem, yet despite malnutrition and starvation of over one billion people our efforts to eliminate these social injustices have been primarily limited to phrases like "the new economic order", etc., which I can assure you do not fill empty stomachs.
Computer technology has unquestionably added to the affluence of our society. However, its infringement on the privacy of individuals has not evoked an adequate response from the political institutions and we have not developed the intellectual perception to measure its future impact.
Medicine has not escaped the technological revolution. In many respects the technological explosion in health services has been far greater than that experienced in other disciplines and, not unexpectedly, has been accompanied by political and moral questions that remain unanswered.
We have seen substantial development of scientific methods capable of shaping the political values of individuals, or what is sometimes commonly referred to as brainwashing. These measures, both physical and psychological, will undoubtedly be developed and refined in future years.
More profound is the likely development of the science of adapting the human personality by chemical and surgical means. It is presently an established fact that certain personality defects can be eliminated by such methods. The consequences of these developments are profound, yet I see little thought given to such matters by governments or, indeed, by those governed. The rapid evolution of the science of genetics poses serious political and moral issues which remain unanswered.
If these examples seem somewhat futuristic, let me assure you they are not. I think all I need do today is mention such topics as organ transplants, artificial insemination, lifesaving systems, euthanasia or abortion, and I am sure I could elicit an immediate response and obviously an immediate debate.

We must recognize that advance in knowledge cannot be suppressed, and yet this is precisely the impression the government is conveying to the scientific community and the public by failing to respond to the aspirations of the scientists on the one hand, and failing to develop the institutions to deal with this knowledge on the other hand. I want to remind all hon. members in this House that in the past when suppressive tactics have been utilized or attempted to be employed, such action has invariably failed.
Demand for knowledge is as much a part of man's nature as is this spirit for adventure. What is needed is derection and purpose, and these will only emanate when we exert an equally profound effort to advance our knowledge and develop our political institutions in concert with scientific advancement. This is the government's challenge if we are to develop a meaningful science policy for Canada. In my opinion the government has failed in that challenge.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the question in the motion before us deals with two primary points, industrial research and development, and academic research. Members who preceded me have talked of both of these areas and I think those who will follow will do the same, dealing I hope more specifically with the academic side, which I do not propose to deal with in a substantial way in my speech.
The first point I should like to make is a more general one in connection with the problem governments have with priorities; that is, where they are going to spend their money.
Quite obviously it seems to me, from my experience here in the House of Commons since 1968, the opposition-in fact I think all politicians at every level-spend very much of their time paying lip service to the need for governments to spend less money. They do this on every occasion, yet when you look at this in hard cold terms here in the House of Commons it is quite evident that the same people, in practically every area, are trying constantly to get the government to spend more and more money. I do not think they can have it both ways.
It is unfortunate the public do not really see us as we really are. They hear the statements we make on television blasting the government for high expenditures. They hear such statements directly in their communities, but they do not see the reality here in the House of Commons where those same people are talking out of a different side of their mouths compared with what they say to the public. It is very important that the public begin to realize that they cannot have it both ways either.
In terms of research and development there is no question but that it is very important. However, so is every other area of government activity. I do not think there is any doubt that we ought to look after our senior citizens, that we ought to look after those who are sick and in hospitals, that we have to look after our veterans, as well as problems in respect of industrial and academic research. We have to do all these things. It is not very fair or very constructive to turn around and zero in on one narrow area in one particular debate, pointing out that we should be spending more money, without at the same time telling us

;

where we should be spending less in order to get additional funds to put into that particular area of activity.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the remarks of the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker). I must admit I have always found him to be a very attentive member of this House, particularly when I am speaking. I do not know whether it is because he wishes to attack me later on or whether he agrees with what I say. However, I have no complaint and I appreciate the comments he makes.
I was talking about the work done by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce in connection with research and development. There is no doubt that no other department, in a government of whatever political party, deserves more credit than the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is one of the best departments in government in attempting to deal effectively with the business community. When I say this I do not mean to imply that I agree with everything done by this department, but by and large its programs are well conceived, well implemented, and have accomplished great things, I think, for the advancement of industry and industrial development in this country.
I might mention the Industrial Research and Development Incentives Act and the program which flows from that act in which the government becomes involved in expanding scientific research and development which might be of significant benefit to Canada, if successful. This particular program involves itself with the private
Science Policy
sector in a very significant way. In the past five years over $150 million has been expended by the Government of Canada directly in respect of the private sector in order to assist it in this area of activity so that it might expand its industrial research and development to create job opportunities, advancements in our economy, and thus help the private sector as well. I think that program has been quite successful.
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has the PAIT program, the program for the advancement of industrial technology. This is designed to assist Canadian industry develop new or improved products, processes or services, which incorporate an advancement in technology and offer good prospects for commercial exploitation. This program is being used very widely by the industrial sector in Canada. Over $135 million has been expended in this area in the last five years. These are both good programs.
I think one of the unfortunate things in respect of both these programs and other programs the department has is that very often the small business community does not have the expertise to go after these programs, to make out the applications, and pursue them sometimes at considerable cost. Too much of these benefits is left with the large industrial organizations. That is a problem which I believe the government recognizes. I certainly do. It is an area of activity in which we as individual members of parliament can become quite involved in order to bring these programs to the attention of small businessmen so that they can take advantage of them. I know that as a result of initiative taken in my area, in co-operation with the federal government, we have managed to bring that lesson down to the small business sector. This has been quite effective with people who normally would not have used these programs.
There is also the program called the Defence Industry Productivity Program which is designed to assist Canadian industry in developing and sustaining its technological capability to supply defence requirements on a competitive basis under the Canada-U.S. defence products sharing program. This program too has been very widely used. In that area we have contributed to the private sector in excess of $240 million in the past five years. These programs under Industry, Trade and Commerce, and many others which I do not need to outline today, are an indication of the importance the government attaches to industrial research and development.
My rough estimate would indicate that the amount of money we have spent in the private sector, or which we are proposing to spend in the private sector, in the 1975-76 fiscal year in this area alone is nearly $300 million. We also spend, in terms of research and development work, about $950 million on in-house laboratory work related to scientific activity through the National Research Council, the Department of National Health and Welfare, and others. This is a large amount of money to be spent on research and development. I am pleased that we are spending that amount.
I will say, however, I am a little disappointed that we have not moved more quickly in the area of transferring amounts of money from in-house research and development into the private sector directly. The policy has been laid down by the former minister of industry, trade and

May 13, 1976
Science Policy
commerce that this is the general approach and direction of the government in the future. I know that the wheels of government move slowly, but I would hope the new Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) would follow the example established by his predecessor and move quickly to move this kind of research back to the private sector, where I think it can be done more effectively and efficiently. There might be more benefit in the private sector than we would perhaps generate by doing it in-house.
In addition to this, there is a fair amount of money, I think about $200 million, spent on university grants and scholarships in the non-profit sector for research and development. All in all the contribution of the government on an annual basis of about $l'/2 billion toward research and development is a large amount of money in anyone's language. I think it could be argued that the amount should be greater, but I think there are just as many arguments that it should be less in a time of restraint. These are value judgments all of us have to make as individual members of parliament concerning where the priority should be.
I am relatively satisfied that the priority given to research and development has been reasonable in a time of restraint. If we spend a lot more money there might be significant benefits from it. But like all research, of course no one knows what the pay-off is until after the money is spent. That is the very nature of research work. There is never any certainty even whether there will be a pay-off. To put more than $1.5 billion into that area at this time with the risks that are involved seems to me perhaps to be going too far.
In addition to the money that is spent by the government itself, in the neighbourhood of $1.5 billion, there is a large amount of money spent by the private sector. It is estimated that in 1975 in excess of $700 million was spent on research in the private sector by the industrial community. You might wonder why I would bring this up when we are really debating the amounts of money contributed by the government itself. I do so because there are special arrangements under the Income Tax Act for fast write-offs in connection with money spent on research and development, which amount to about a 40 per cent contribution, which means that of that $706 million spent in the private sector alone the government is contributing in excess of $300 million in special tax write-offs in order to allow it to do that kind of work.
There is a lot of money being spent on research and development, but there is obviously room for spending a lot more. I think that when our economy is in a condition where we can allow an increase in government expenditures, some consideration should be given to accelerating the expenditures in this area of activity, but at present I am totally satisfied that the amount we are spending, particularly in the industrial sector, which I have talked about most in my few remarks today, is a reasonable amount.
Perhaps in some way we could get more benefit without spending more money, but I would simply make one point to the government for consideration. A large section of our research funds is provided by way of grants, some of which 
range up to 90 per cent of the cost of a research project, and some go down as low as 25 per cent. I think there would be some merit if the government were to consider giving less in grants in certain specialized areas, where it ends up giving low interest loans to many corporations which wish to get involved in research and development and which are quite confident they will have an economic pay-off in the immediate future, and cease to put money out with no expectation of return. I hope that the government, particularly the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, will give some consideration to adopting such an approach.
I have spoken to many large and small businessmen who praise these programs quite highly, but at the same time many of them say that what they are really looking for is access to funds. They say they cannot get funds at a reasonable cost in order to make high risk investments in research and development.
