Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this motion introduced by the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling), for one area of government failure has been in its allocation of funds for fisheries research.
May 13, 1976

When the Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc) appeared before the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry on March 30 he stated that the estimated cost of carrying out the fisheries and marine program of the government amounted to slightly over $261 million of which some $155 million would be used for operating expenditures, while just over $113 million would be devoted to fisheries management and research and while some $42 million would be allocated to support activities related to ocean and aquatic sciences. On the surface this would appear to be an aggressive program. To someone looking at it for the first time it looks quite large. It is not unlike looking at an iceberg which looms large at first glance, until it is realized that nine tenths of its size are beneath the surface. The amount made available by the government for the fishing industry is readily comparable to an iceberg, for the basic needs of nine tenths of this important industry are, unfortunately, being ignored by this government.
I say this because the fishing industry is one of Canada's most important assets. It is vital to the livelihood not only of the residents of Atlantic Canada, not only of the residents of central and western Canada, but also to the livelihood of many people residing up and down the entire length of the Pacific coast.
The commercial landed value of the 1974 fisheries harvest, for example, was estimated to be close to $500 million and, of course, the resale value of this resource was much greater than that figure. Canada needs a viable, vibrant, strong and healthy fishing industry because it is the fisheries which provide employment opportunities in many areas of Canada where there are no alternative employment opportunities. In order to bring this about, constant, and I realize, expensive ongoing research is not only necessary, but I say mandatory. Unfortunately this government has not seen fit to maintain and staff an adequate research department, and this is reflected in the decline of our fisheries and those employed by the industry in all areas of Canada.
When I look at the Blue Book of estimates for this year, I cannot help but question the spending priorities of this government. I cannot help but ask how it is more important to be entertained than it is to be fed and to be employed. The minister mentioned, for example, that of $261 million for the government's fishing and marine program, $42 million was to go toward ocean and aquatic sciences. This is little more than half the amount made available to the CBC this year, which spends all it takes in from any particular area and which still requires a handout from the public purse in the amount of $416 million. This is some $63 million more than it required just a year ago. Yet the quality of CBC productions and, I might add, the record of service of its employees, seem to deteriorate in direct relation to its increased budget.
When I state my views concerning the lack of research funds for the fishing industry I am not alone in this stand. The Fisheries Research Bureau complained in its report of February, 1976, that the research planning, programming, and funding procedures with respect of Canada's fisheries resources are in a state of chaos. In fact out of a total
Science Policy
budget of $261 million the Fisheries Department has allocated only pennies to its research program.
Salvation for the fishing industry could well come in the form of a 200 mile limit. The government has stated that such a limit is mandatory for the good health of our fisheries, yet this self-same government has delayed and is continuing to delay putting this 200 mile limit into effect. Canada needs this limit, and needs it now. We need the research to manage intelligently the harvest of fish within the limit as well as to extract the possible oil, gas and minerals which may exist on the continental shelf.
Canada once had a national research institution, the Fisheries Research Board, with a network of laboratories, and granting functions. This has recently been taken apart, however, and the pieces have not yet been put together in an alternative, viable structure.
A number of senior scientists have retired, and a university grant program has been transformed into a process in which university scientists are expected to serve as junior assistants to younger scientists in the federal field. As a result, at a time when Canada needs effective scientific studies on fisheries resources, the industry finds itself without an appropriate institutional structure to stimulate, guide, and achieve scientific success.
As well as the problems raised by insufficient research there are certain problems with the research that does exist. I believe that too much of our fisheries research effort is being diverted to manipulate coarse data into simple models with little objective reliability. For many stocks, herring, for example, maps of various stages of their life history are totally inadequate. Monitoring is in a difficult state in that the accuracy of statistics and landings for all countries is suspect; data on area of capture may well be falsified; technical samplings for sizes and ages both landed and caught are inadequate, and sizes and kinds of fish being discarded are unreported.
I have a letter dated March 11, 1976, from Professor K. H. Mann, chairman of the Department of Biology at Dalhousie University, regarding Canada's research effort. He states:
I wish to draw your attention to the steady erosion of support for research in the universities through the National Research Council. During 1969-75 NRC funds increased, on average, less than 2 per cent per annum, and our present research grants are now worth, in real buying power, 41 per cent less than in 1969. Since most basic research is done in universities, this means a serious cutback in fundamental studies of problems of importance to Canada. We cannot argue that Canada can apply to its own problems the basic research done elsewhere. My own research is an example. We are studying the fundamental problems of the ecology of lobsters. This work is not being done anywhere else in the world. Lobsters do not occur on the Pacific coast, nor in waters south of New York. Hence there are very few first class laboratories with facilities to study the problems of the lobster fishery. We are told that provision has been made for the government to award contracts through the Department of the Environment, but in 1974-75 there were no contracts in biology which were on topics suggested by the university professors. This was in a year when the government spent $110 millions on intradepartmental research on biological and medical topics, and $6 million on research contracts.
I find this position most alarming, and trust that you will share my concern and take appropriate action.
We certainly share his concern, for lobsters are among the largest dollar earners in Atlantic Canada. From the efforts of the Minister of State (Fisheries) to curtail the catch, we know there is considerable concern over the decline in stocks.

Science Policy
Certainly we know quite a bit about the lobster and its growth. One of the difficulties about raising it in captivity is its cannablistic tendencies. Come scientists have discovered, however, that by putting each lobster in a separate compartment and feeding it, it is possible to raise it from the larvae stage to a saleable age of four or five years. I hope the minister will seriously reconsider the amount of funds available for the development and improvement of our lobster stocks which provide so much of the income for inshore fishermen in Atlantic Canada.
The time for action on these problems was yesterday- not some foggy time in the future which may well be too late. In the recently released publication entitled "Policy for Canada's Commercial Fisheries" the need for more and better research is briefly mentioned twice. It states that Canada needs a co-ordinated research and administrative capability to control fishery resource use on an ecological basis and in accordance with the best interests, economic and social, of Canadian society. It also states that there is a need to provide the research and the institutional innovation necessary to foster the development of viable aquacul-tural enterprise. Although it could be construed that these two vague ramblings denote that fisheries officials recognize the problem, there is still no evidence that the present government plans to meet and challenge it.
I brought up this problem about the lack of research in the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry on April 27, 1976. Witnesses from the department continually wanted to stress that their research on east coast redfish is unequalled. They were not as willing to talk about research on the other fish stocks, however. In light of the fact that there are some 60 different stocks on the east coast, that leaves some 59 stocks without adequate research.
We might ask what the economic result is of this inadequate research, Mr. Speaker. A regulation was passed on February 26, 1976-without consultation with any of the provincial governments-which I submit may well be a contravention of the British North America Act. There was no consultation with any provincial premier on this matter which could well put some of the major fishing ports in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia out of business. Why are we not managing all the other species that are in serious trouble, and in some areas are almost wiped out?
Statistics indicate landings of 23,946 metric tons of all ground fish species in the first two months of this year, of which 12,096 metric tons was ocean perch. Perch has been the backbone of the TRAWLER fleet and is the species required to give the volumes necessary to keep the all year round ports open. Existing government assistance programs will not overcome the increased costs due to the effect on overhead of decreased volumes.
To the Atlantic redfish regulations, codfish caught in the Gulf have now been added. The redfish regulations make second class Canadians of Newfoundlanders and Nova Scotians. I say this because of some of the rules and regulations laid down. In light of the time limitation I shall not read all of them, but I should like to place one on the record which was Gazetted on February 26, one day before government officials called representatives of the industry together to get their views on what should be done. Mr. Speaker, this is hypocrisy in high places.

One of the rules states:
No person shall use any vessel that is more than 100 feet in length over-all to fish for redfish in the Gulf of St. Lawrence if the port from which that vessel operated prior to February 1, 1976 is situated outside the Gulf of St. Lawrence.
The owner of a ship of 100 feet in length based in the Gulf of St. Lawrence may continue fishing, but a Newfoundland captain or a Nova Scotian captain is unable to continue fishing in the Gulf of St. Lawrence. I say this regulation makes second class citizens of Newfoundlanders and Nova Scotians. Either we are all Canadians, with equal rights in this country, or we in Atlantic Canada are being discriminated against in legislation. I submit this regulation is unfair. It is unjust. I personally hope that changes will be made in future regulations of this type.
One may ask on what were these regulations based? I say that they were based on the inadequate assessment of L. S. Parsons and D. G. Parsons of Environment Canada. I do not wish to place the entire assessment on record. The first paragraph states that this was "a directed fishery". The quality and quantity of redfish stocks in the 1948-50 era was such that they were capable of sustaining a very heavy fishery. The report suggested that the people in Atlantic Canada should build fleets sufficiently large to take advantage of these stocks. This was done. Many large operators decided to expand their fleets in size and number, to take advantage of these stocks. They did this on the basis of the report submitted by L. S. Parsons and D. G. Parsons of Environment Canada, fisheries and marine service, Newfoundland Biological Station, at St. John's, Newfoundland.
The first sentence of the last paragraph on page 1 of the report reads in part:
... intensification of fishing pressure on redfish in the Gulf created concern about overfishing.
Later in the paragraph one sees the words "based on limited data." On the basis of limited data it was concluded that the red fishery conducted in recent years should be concluded. Because of limited data some companies may well be put out of business.
When Canada declares a 200-limit she will then be responsible for managing and allotting quotas within that area. Fisheries has stated that it plans to give Canadian fishermen as much quota as they need. Foreign fishermen would take the rest. However, is Canada presently in a position to determine what the quota levels should be? The Fisheries Council of Canada does not think so. Nor does ICNAF, which has stated that Canada does not have the necessary boats or manpower to collect adequately the needed data on the numbers and breeding patterns of the fish stocks within the 200-mile limit. Mr. K. C. Lucas of the Ministry of Fisheries said in committee that more funds for research were needed. He stated:
You do not mount a research program overnight. You also do not get the results overnight. The results are probably five to ten years in coming. It is certainly something that we ... will be asking government, and bringing to their attention the fact that we will need, in particular, after extension of jurisdiction, substantial new resources both in operating funds and in terms of vessels and equipment to do a decent job of stock assessment so that we can, in fact, make better predictions and make better regulations for the harvesting of the stocks.
May 13, 1976

On the other hand I would say that these additional funds are needed now, not later. What Canadian fishermen gain by having a 200-mile limit could be lost by the government's inability to know and to preserve what we have out there.
Finally, our lack of research is costing us dearly in yet another field, in the lack of technology in developing a capability for mining the resources, mineral, oil and gas, on our continental shelf.
On Tuesday, May 11, as reported at page 11386 of Hansard, I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) about the U.S. proposal to mine some 6 per cent of its nickel requirements from the nodules on the seabed, and what our response was to this proposal. The minister replied that we opposed it. Mr. Speaker, we cannot continue to bury our head in the sand, and cannot continue to ignore new technological developments merely because we in Canada choose to be penny wise and pound foolish.
It is predicted that the mineral resources of the sea will provide great wealth in future, once technological processes to extract them are developed. One example is the five million tons of gold said t* exist in the ocean. At present large amounts of petrolfeum and natural gas are being extracted from the oceans. Approximately 18.5 per cent of world oil production now comes from off-shore wells. This proportion is expected to increase by another 14 per cent within the next ten years. An estimated 2,500 billion barrels of liquid fuels are potentially recoverable from off-shore areas of the world, and some of this potential is believed to exist on our own continental shelf.
Phosphate deposits, which may eventually refurbish the supply of fertilizer phosphates, have been found off the coasts of the U.S.A., the west coasts of south and Central America, and off Argentina, Japan, and South Africa. Of course we do not know if there are any deposits off the coasts of Canada because we have not the research funds with which to find them.
I submit that manganese deposits hold the most immediate promise of reward for exploration. Plans are well advanced for the building of a plant in the Gulf of Mexico area which is to handle one million tons of nodules a year, from a 4,000 square mile mine site discovered between the continental U.S.A. and Hawaii. This operation is planned to yield 260,000 tons of manganese, 12,600 tons of nickel,
10,000	tons of copper, and 2,400 tons of cobalt per year.
As with other resources of the sea, the conflict in positions is between those with the capacity to exploit resources and those without such capacities. I submit that unless we make more funds available for research and development we may not only lose more of our fisheries resources but stand to lose our potential oil, gas, and mineral reserves, owing to our lack of technology for finding them and making them available not only to Canadians but to all mankind.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join with others who have spoken today in commending the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) for putting down the motion which is the subject of debate and which covers all areas of research. I suppose one could contend that just about everything that
Science Policy
needs to be said has been put on record, but I welcome this opportunity to speak for a few minutes as I wish to emphasize an area of research which I feel deserves a better break than the government has been giving it. I refer to the entire field of medical research.
Sir, Canada's contribution to medical research over the years has been tremendous. In recent years, in large measure owing to government funding, there have been assembled in our universities in particular, and in our medical institutions, teams of research workers who have enthusiastically been doing research on some diseases which are yet to be conquered and on ways and means to improve our environment, our diet, and all the things which make for healthy living for Canadians and, indeed, for human beings all over the world.
I think I can say that most of us in this House are disheartened because the so-called restraint program under which we are asked to live is being unfairly applied to medical research. In some cases amounts available are being frozen, in others they are being dropped, with the result that many teams working on medical research projects will very likely be dismantled or cease doing the valuable work they have in hand.
We are aware of some of the killers still with us, cancer and heart disease; we are aware of cripplers which still need to be mastered, such as arthritis and multiple sclerosis. We are aware that many diseases we thought hit only older people hit younger persons, even children. Surely, Sir, in this field in which Canada has done so much in the past, we should carry on in that tradition. I regard it as disastrous that the fine young men and women in our universities and medical schools who have shown such devotion to medical research are being discouraged by the present policies of the government.
I am interested in the various areas of research which have been discussed today during the course of this debate. They are all important. Next to medical research, I regard as extremely important research into things that relate to the environment, to the provisions of food of such dietary quality that it makes for good health and, indeed, all that goes to raising the standard of health of our people. When we talk about medical research and the health of Canadians, and the health of human beings generally, we talk about things that are extremely important.
I rise for these few minutes in this debate to join in the plea that was made earlier today by my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), and to emphasize the plea that we have made repeatedly, that the government desist from applying its restraint program to medical research.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext: Cease and desist.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext:
My hon. friend with his legal background wants me to use the phrase "cease and desist". In plain language, I want the government to stop it.
I know the government has a restraint program. When you see how money is spent in some cases, you are not sure that the government is aware that it has a restraint pro-

May 13, 1976
Science Policy
gram. But in any kind of program there should be common sense. Just because the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) is selling the idea that everything should be cut down is no reason why particular programs should not be looked at and the realization admitted that those programs should not be cut back or should even be expanded. You can cut back on some things and save a few dollars and, when the restraint period is over and the money supply goes up, there has been no great harm. However, if you cut back or abandon research programs, and our top scientists and medical students go to other countries, the loss down the road can be incalculable. We will never be able to measure it. We will never know what discoveries, in terms of conquering disease or promoting good health, were lost because of this disastrous, ridiculous restraint program that is being applied in this area.
When you put my name on the list, Mr. Speaker, you asked me whether I would take my full time. I said no, I just wanted a few minutes. I have said what I wanted to say. I want the government to have some common sense, to remove the restraint program from medical research, and to give medical research and those engaged in it the opportunity to carry on the good work they have pursued over the years.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Fleming (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope in the next few minutes I might attempt, by describing certain activities within the Department of Communications, to outline very much a thrust by the Government of Canada in its science policy, more particularly by the Department of Communications, to do just the contrary of what today's motion accuses the government of doing. In fact I hope in the next few minutes, by developing on a particular theme, Canada's new communications technology satellite, I might prove that in fact the Canadian government is adopting measures that will increase research and development in both the industrial and academic communities of Canada.
I would like first to outline some basic details of the communications technology satellite. It is an experimental satellite which was placed in space early this year from the Kennedy Space Centre in Florida. CTS, as it is called, is seen as the advanced technology forerunner of a new breed of high-powered orbitting transmitters expected to provide a wide range of expanded communications services in the 1980's. It is the product of more than five years of work by Canadian government officials and Canadian industry space scientists and engineers. The work of those people over five years was a forerunner in the world.
The primary objectives of the CTS program are to demonstrate high powered television and other transmission to small and other low cost earth stations. That is one of the primary purposes and in itself will be a revolution, not only for Canada but for earth stations and radio station technology around the world. Further, one of the intentions of the CTS program is to flight-test major advanced technology subsystems of the spacecraft itself. The program is to develop further and demonstrate the abilities of the Canadian industry in the design and fabrication of subsystems and components for the space/com-munications systems of tomorrow.

With a design life of two years, the $60 million satellite is being used for a series of social, technological and technical communications experiments by various groups on both sides of the Canada-U.S. border.
The CTS is being orbitted under a continuing program of Canada-United States collaboration in the peaceful uses of outer space that began with the 1962 launch of Alouette-1. Some hon. members may recall that the functioning of Alouette-1, the first satellite put into space by any nation other than the two superpowers, brought great credit and esteem to Canada and Canada's space scientists from countries around the world.
Canada designed and built the CTS spacecraft. The United States, after providing its high powered transmitting tube and free-launch test support, carried out the launch. The European Space Agency also participated through a bilateral agreement with Canada. I should point out that the satellite itself is more than 90 per cent Canadian produced and made up of Canadian components. As I began by saying, this is the most powerful communications satellite in space.
Canadian experimenter groups, whose interests encompass the fields of broadcasting technology, telemedicine, tele-education, community interaction, data transmission, and government operations in remote areas, will carry out experiments during the two year lifespan of CTS. Experimenters include several major universities in central Canada and the maritimes, the Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba governments, the CBC, Bell Canada, Telesat Canada, the Alberta Native Communications Society and the Rural Health Society of Victoria, B.C. When the charge is made by the opposition that the government is not adopting measures that will increase research and development in both the industrial and academic communities, they are overlooking this program. As I just read out, the people, companies, associations, academic community and political interests that will be involved, it is indeed broadly adjusting and interesting all the various scientific sectors in its program.
CTS is the first to operate in the new 12 and 14 Gigahertz satellite frequency bands allocated by the International Telecommunications Union. It incorporates three major advanced technology subsystems which are in themselves important experiments. If I may, I will just mention those systems.
The first is a pair of lighweight, flexible solar power arrays or "sails", to provide an initial power output of about 1,200 watts. It is those sails and, through the performance of them expanding in space, moving outward and revealing to the sun the solar cells, that in fact makes this satellite the most powerful communications satellite in space. I might say it is a totally Canadian owned company that was encouraged to carry out that technology as the result of the planning done on the CTS. The company in particular is Spar Aerospace of Toronto.
Another major advanced technology subsystem is a travelling wave tube amplifier of approximately 50 per cent efficiency with an output power of about 200 watts and a three-axis stabilization system designed to maintain high antenna pointing accuracy in spite of the flexing of the solar arrays.
May 13, 1976

While people around the world may well think of the United States and Russia as landing people on the moon and going into the far distances of outer space, Canada is right up there with the major powers of the world in modern communications and space technology, and the reason for that is the long run planning of the Government of Canada through its Ministry of Science and Technology, and especially because of the efforts of the Department of Communications and the ministers who have been in charge of that department.
Mr. Speaker, there are 26 major projects which will be carried out with the help of the communications technology satellite, and to show that the government is acting to increase research and development in both the industrial and academic communities I should like to cite several of the experiments which will take place. One is called radio broadcasting applications. The objectives are to demonstrate the technical feasibility of the satellite CTS for radio broadcasting, its relevance for the extension of radio services between small communities, and its possibilities for providing special interest programming direct to individual broadcasting stations. It is, of course, in the interest of our remote northern communities to receive this specialized programming which takes into consideration the needs of our ethnic peoples and the variety of their backgrounds. This kind of technology will also be of great importance and use for our native people.
A further test on the CTS will consist of television special demonstrations. By transmitting coverage of the 1976 Olympic equestrian competitions from Bromont, Quebec, to Montreal during the period July 17-August 1, it is hoped to determine the suitability of a CTS type spacecraft for remote broadcast and control and transmission reception from large, populated areas, while evaluating the flexibility and handling efficiency of portable ground stations under operational pressures.
One of the experiments is something called "Staff Training By Satellite". This is something of great significance and when we talk about restraint and the need to increase efficiency and reduce government costs. Staff training by satellite is a program where characteristics of satellite operation which might lead to the development of cost-effective, high-speed learning environments for training federal employees in their home offices will be studied. Improved professional development methods will be sought through exploration of new directions for educational TV via satellite.
There will also be telemedicine experiments with CTS. The satellite will be used to provide continuing medical education for doctors and allied health professionals practicing in remote areas by one-way video, with two-way audio. Community health education programs and transmissions of medical data such as electro-cardiograms and X-rays from remote areas will also be assessed. What this means is that in time somebody critically ill with a serious and complicated disease in a remote part of Canada could be quickly analyzed via a satellite in one of our major cities where a leading expert in that area of medicine could, from that vast distance, do his very best to treat a patient who otherwise would not get adequate treatment.
Science Policy
To mention another project, there is what is called the omnibus network. To ensure the widest possible access to higher education in the province, the University of Quebec is decentralized, operating out of regional centres with a telephone network utilized for teaching, management, and document exchange. The experiment using the communications technology satellite of the Government of Canada will test the ability of the satellite to improve this process, stimulating educational satellite applications considered likely to be operational in the 1980's.
Radio telephony with remote camps is another program. One-metre terminals will be used to establish high quality telephone links with remote sites in the James Bay area. The transportability of the terminal, and any change in productivity due to better communications between the head office of the James Bay Development Corporation and survey parties will be assessed.
To get into some of the more technical kind of programs along the scientific rather than the educational and social field, I might mention one or two which CTS will carry out. There are telephony, data transmission and synchronisation studies. The flexibility and reliability of the CTS system to aid in the precise control of remote power stations in Northern Quebec will be determined. At present, high frequency radio links connect such generator sites with a regional despatching centre in Quebec City. During the experimental period clock synchronization as well as voice fascimile and transmission of slow rate data by satellite will be studied.
The Manitoba government computer centre will be involved in a program called the "Government Teleprocessing Network Experiment." Further, a satellite link radio interferometry experiment will be watched by scientists who are keenly interested in the location, distribution, and structure of a number of intense sources of electromagnetic radiation deep in space. The purpose of this experiment is to permit the real time comparison or correlation of signals from such sources as received by different radio telescopes hundreds of miles apart. Much information can be determined or inferred from such comparisons, helping to unravel mysteries surrounding extragalactic radio sources. That is one of the 26 experiments which is to the forefront of the advances being made in space and satellite technology. It is carried out by means of a satellite which has made Canada a world leader, the most powerful communications satellite in space. It is almost entirely Canadian developed and built. It has been built through the work and effort of the Department of Communications, but also by encouraging the private sector. It has made several Canadian companies leaders in particular areas of space research.
In this context I might mention Spar Aerospace of which I spoke earlier, the company which developed the expandable wings which carried the solar cells which supplied power to the satellite and, because of that technology, made it the most powerful in space. In turn, the encouragement of such a company means that in the future when the U.S. government finally puts in place its space shuttle, which is the coming way of placing in orbit satellites, that space shuttle will include as a major part of its equipment an arm developed by Spar Aerospace of Canada, and it will mean that Canada will play a major role in the success of

May 13, 1976
Science Policy
that major space ship, the space shuttle, which is due for launch and eventually for regular use late this decade or early in the 1980's.
There is much more of course that is being carried out by the Department of Communications in relation to the overall science policy for Canada. I might mention particularly the Anik B, the fourth of the Anik series of satellites, which is planned to be launched in about two years in a program undertaken through co-operation between TELE-SAT Canada and the federal Department of Communications. That particular satellite will not only be carrying on its responsibility of providing domestic satellite communications, but it will include as well a 12 and 14 Gigahertz section as well as the traditional 4 and 6 Gigahertz bands in order to continue the CTS program of experimentation so that Canada may continue to be a leader in space Technology.
I might add that at the Shirley's Bay Space Research Centre of the Department of Communications important work is being done to find ways of reducing costs and improving telephone services in rural communities because of the serious problems we face there. As well, through the co-operation and assistance of the Government of Canada and because of the structure in Canada the subsidiary of Bell Canada, Bell Northern, now re-named Northern Telecommunications, has a reputation around the world as a front runner in telephone science and technology.
The motion laid down by the Official Opposition charges that the government has failed to develop a strong science policy or implement measures to increase research and development in the industrial and academic communities. One must always be concerned that every effort be directed toward research in Canada, and research has many various aspects but it seems to me the opposition is forgetting the very real world leadership position Canada has because of the planning of the government in space research and technology.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regard it as an honour to take part in this debate. It is a high level debate that deals with high level and important issues. For a long period of time the science community of Canada have wondered whether the House of Commons would ever turn its attention to the practical problems which beset that community. I suspect they thought their issues carried very little political sex appeal. I suspect also they were pessimistic in that their problems were being ignored by us.
In the last year there have been at last three debates of consequence on the problems of the scientific community. The first debate was launched on June 9 of last year by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre). There was a debate prior to passage of an appropriations bill during which several members expressed a concern in respect of medical research. Now there is the present motion before us today by the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) which gives us another chance to consider something that is especially important.
In looking back at my correspondence from those who wanted to direct my attention to the problems of the scientific community I find they had very little to say to me and I, therefore, to them over most of my parliamentary career. The file I have tonight I find has grown up and developed mostly since the year 1974. I should like to share some of the views, the fears and hopes that are set forth in the letters that comprise this file.
Perhaps it is an obvious point, but one that should be made, that these are thoughtful Canadians capable of forming public opinion, and who do form public opinion, who have written us about their problems. These are bread and butter issues being presented in large terms with long
May 13, 1976

vision, rather than in short terms with immediate vision of self-help for one's own pocket.
I know the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) has talked about scientific research on the late show on a number of occasions, and others in the House have raised these problems from time to time. When something becomes such an issue that it is raised on at least three occasions during special debates in parliament within a year, this surely means there is something wrong.
I listened with great pleasure to the speech of the hon. member who preceded me, the hon. member for York West (Mr. Fleming). After making a clarion call of self-satisfaction and patting the government on the back for what it has done, I still maintain the fact is that more and more people feel the government is not doing enough in this very large field of scientific research and development and technology.
I support the motion of the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth. I am glad he has proposed it, and I suspect many similar motions will be put forward and that members will find it more and more attractive to debate a subject such as science policy than has been the case before last year.
The file I have contains letters from all aspects of research; from experts in biochemistry and in pharmacology, as well as from the University of New Brunswick with its famous forestry school. A copy of one letter addressed to the minister who is the custodian of science and research in Canada, and who is also the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Drury), was forwarded to me.
Let me now move to some specific points of view. I want to present the histories or points of view from particular aspects of research. Since I am a member for part of the Halifax area one might suspect that many of these views would come from the university community there. That is precisely the case. They come from Dalhousie University, the medical college of which stands a few blocks away from my home. When you read letters such as this you realize some of the attributes and qualities that go into the making of a first-class research person, some of whom are also able to put the language into pretty glittering terms.
The first quotation I have contains one of the finest pieces of writing that has ever crossed my desk as a member of parliament. It comes from three members of the Department of Biology of Dalhousie University, Professors K. H. Mann, E. C. Pielou, and L. C. Vining. These gentlemen, involved collectively in biological research, state in part:
We are alarmed at the steady decline in government support for basic scientific research. As evidence we point to the fact that since 1970 the funds allocated to the National Research Council to support research in universities (where most basic studies are done) have increased only 5 per cent while in the same period the Gross National Product has increased 49 per cent and the Consumer Price Index by 29 per cent. Moreover we are falling behind in comparison with other developed nations: in the period in which our expenditure on basic research rose by 5 per cent, that of Britain, France and the U.S. increased by about 50 per cent.
The argument that belt-tightening is unavoidable in the present economic state of the world and that basic research ought to be sacrificed to short-term problem solving ("mission-oriented" or applied research, as it is called) is most shortsighted.
Science Policy
Brace yourself now, because here is the line that so took my fancy:
It would be as sensible to advocate cutting off the roots of apple trees since, as any fool knows, apples grow on the branches, not the roots.
My friends continue:
The problem solving functions of science that are now so urgent (because of the energy crisis, the population crisis, the world food shortage, the environmental crisis, and all the other crises that beset us) will falter unless there is a steady advance in basic science to nourish them. Everyone in this country daily uses products derived from the basic research of the past.
Anyone who uses a telephone, a radio, or a TV, is using a device that could never have been invented without the basic knowledge of electromagnetism gained beforehand. Anyone who benefits from modern medicine, who flies in a modern plane, or who merely eats a modern load of bread, is profiting from basic research carried out some time previously. The dependence of our civilization on scientific knowledge is so taken for granted that it is forgotten.
That is the letter from the three professors of the Department of Biology at Dalhousie University. I think they make the point as effectively and as tellingly as it can be made. One of the students, Gynheung An, also entered another piece of correspondence. He pointed out the following in his letter:
Our basic budget has now been frozen at $12.4 million for 1976/77 while the Biological Council of Canada recommended a basic budget of $18.5 million-
By very quick arithmetic that is approximately 50 per cent more.
-and the Science Council recommended $19.9 million for the same period.
That, by a quick calculation, is more than 50 per cent. The student continues:
As things stand now, over 60 per cent of the funds allocated through NRC are spent on graduate student support and technicians' salaries. A freeze at the present inadequate level of support is thus unjustified.
Professor Vining, writing for himself and not in association with his two other colleagues, wrote me the following about two months ago:
We in the universities are seeing a rapid erosion of the value of our research grants as the cost of equipment and services skyrockets. To quote an example, a roll of dialysis tubing purchased in 1974 for $14.18 last week cost me $45.76 on re-order. Much of my NRC research grant is spent on salaries for technicians, summer student assistants or postgraduate associates. A freeze on research funds means that I can increase salaries for some to cope with inflation only at the cost of dismissing others. Highly trained people forced into unemployment in the present job market must seek other occupations and soon lose their skills.
All of this makes worse an already difficult position for university research in the biological sciences. In 1974/76 NRC handled 1546 grant requests in biology and was unable to fund 22.5 per cent of them (the rejection rate was 0 per cent in nuclear physics and only 12 per cent in physics as a whole). A high proportion of university professors in biology departments are unable to undertake research and the university teaching environment has suffered accordingly.
Finally, because I know there are other speakers and I would hope that everyone who wishes to participate will have that opportunity, this point is made by Professor S. D. Wainwright, President of the Canadian Society for Cell Biology at Dalhousie University, and a member of the Department of Biochemistry:
In my own case for example, of a total of $56,000 awarded by the NRC for the fiscal year 1975-76 approximately $36,700 will go toward salaries,

May 13, 1976
Science Policy
etc., for four employees. The balance is used for purchase of equipment and other supplies which are purchased from local dealers and agents as far as is possible. Actual proportions of grants spent on salaries and on supplies will vary for different grantees, and will on the average probably be less for faculty receiving the smaller average grants from NRC. Nevertheless, the over-all situation for all grants combined here, as in other parts of Canada, will correspond roughly with that for my own grants.
Time will not permit me to read all of the letter, but later he states:
The more severely the graduate programmes at Dalhousie are crippled by reductions in effective support for scientific research, the greater will be the future dependence of this region upon research scientists trained elsewhere (i.e. the U.S.A.). Indeed, it seems possible that in many areas Dalhousie would be unable to offer any graduate programme at all.
What a pity that would be because the history of that great university has been built in new directions and now is threatened with loss of some of the programs which have been won through an immense amount of effort and money. Those are examples, Mr. Speaker.
I can see at least three evils if correction is not undertaken. First, there is the very obvious one that what is lost will take years to recover. If an important scientific establishment is dismantled or crippled, the effects can be devastating not only in the short run but in the long run as well. The second thing is that the United States, with all its economic and other difficulties, which are as major as the economic difficulties of Canada, is doing a much better job of showing respect for scientific research. The inevitable result is that many scientists will be working in the United States who will have stamped on their personalities the expression "Made in Canada". Finally, we will lose thereby some of our industrial and scientific strength.
I think this all indicates that it behooves us not only to debate this question today but to take a good long hard look at it, and try perhaps as a parliament to do a selling job in some areas. We must go about the business of raising money by taxes and spending it, and I happen to think this is one of the areas in which this should be done.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the particularly warm applause I heard from the other side of the House. I know it is heartfelt.
I must say it was a privilege to have been in the House during virtually all of today to listen to the contributions made during this debate. Like some other members I am grateful that the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) brought down this motion, the general topic of which I approve, or at least the first sentence or so in it. In the second part the hon. member appears perhaps somewhat to have lost his sense of balance and has engaged in what is meaningless, partisan rhetoric.
I do think it is useful from time to time for as distinguished a body as this to turn its attention to some of the problems facing science, the scientific community, the de-

velopment and application of technology in this country. Everyone is agreed, it is quite clear, that both science and technology are immensely significant, immensely important in the development not only of our prosperity as it is generally understood but also, and perhaps equally, in the preservation and enhancement of the environment and the quality of our life. Understanding this, the government has introduced a number of policies and programs, some of which have been described to the House, mostly, I must confess, by supporters on this side. The details given indicate quite clearly that the regrets expressed by the hon. member who moved the motion are really without any adequate foundation.
I would point out that we in the government look at science and technology or research under three headings. One is the support of science or the support of research essential in the pursuit of science, in its broader sense meaning knowledge. In this respect the government does make a significant contribution to advancing the frontiers of knowledge in this country, principally through the instrumentality of universities, and both to create this effort and to sustain it there are three councils: the National Research Council, the Medical Research Council, and the Canada Council, all three of which dispense annually substantial sums of money in support of research almost entirely in the universities.
The purpose of this research is two-fold. First, it is recognized that higher education in order to be fresh and good must provide a field for its teachers to advance continually their own state of knowledge in order better to be able to pass it on to their students, and second, the general advancement of knowledge, of research outside the straight teaching function. Here is a field in which the three guiding councils I have mentioned have interested themselves. They have sums, voted by parliament, made available to them annually, and these are distributed among the classical disciplines according to the judgments made as to appropriateness in size and destination by peer groups, that is, members of the scientific community who themselves are knowledgeable in the particular field.
This year, as a consequence of the general policies of restraint which have been visited on and by the government, the increases over last year of funds available to these three councils have been very modest indeed. They have been less than the increase in inflation this year over last. As a consequence, there has to be a restraining of effort and ambitions, as indeed is the case in most other sectors of the economy, and perhaps research to devise ways of accomplishing more for less in the way of resources.
I think that most of us would agree that periodically such an exercise is both intellectually and economically a healthy one. I suggest, however, that it cannot be maintained indefinitely or it will have the result of running down what up to the present has been a first class product, a first class effort in Canada, which is internationally acknowledged.
This then is the year of restraint and, as I think a good number of hon. members are aware, this has caused a great deal of heart searching, and indeed in many cases considerable difficulty in the academic community. We are aware of this and we sympathize, but it is difficult to achieve a

universal policy of restraint visited with fairness on all the citizenry of Canada without anyone having in any way to suffer.
It would be my hope that the kind of severe restrictions under which we are labouring this year will not be continued indefinitely. Indeed I am sure it would be harmful if they were. However, there is one thing I should like to say. I have said that the purpose of this research is to enhance the teaching in institutions of higher learning. We are not too sure how many of what particular kinds of training will be needed in the future in Canada.
It will be an endeavour of the government during the course of the current year to establish a study looking into the future to try to see if we can find out with more certainty what will be the kinds of university training, what will be the kinds of university produced skills which are most likely to be in demand in Canada in the next ten to 15 years. If we can do this, then we will be able to arrive at a rather more intelligent guidance for our young people either entering university or contemplating, following a general arts or science course, specializing in post-graduate work, to provide them with a little more in the way of guidance than we have been able to do in the past. This would avoid the situation which we seem to run into periodically of facing shortages of engineers, of doctors in particular lines, or of physicists, and then rushing to find them abroad or to take half-trained people to do the jobs, whereas if we had looked ahead more intelligently the shortages could have been anticipated, planned for, and met. Equally, we hope we will not be in the position of having surpluses of perhaps narrowly trained men or women coming out of universities into what would be an over-crowded avocation or profession.
Unfortunately, however, I do not expect that we can be very successful in much less than a year in producing such a forecast for the future. I have invited a number of people in the academic world to participate in this, and hopefully the results will not only be useful but indeed important in getting the kind of resources put into, through these granting councils, the universities, to match the resources needed for the particular job of training, which we can contemplate with a little more certainty than we have been able to do in the past.
In addition to those policies and programs in support of research we have a number of policies and programs for the application of research, science, and technology to the solution of non scientific problems or general problems. Rather than constituting an end or aim in itself, science and technology are tools which, if they are useful and productive, can and should be used.
I see it as one of the tasks of the ministry, about which there has been some complaint, to ensure that in attacking the problems which the various departments of the federal government face that scientific tools are available for use by them if they can be effectively and efficiently utilized in the solution of these problems. In some cases this is so; in other cases it is not. However, as one hon. member pointed out, there has been much discovered and much new knowledge acquired at an ever accelerating pace. One of the tasks of the ministry is to see that this new knowl-
Science Policy
edge is available to other departments of the Government of Canada in the solution of their problems.
Equally, it would be the choice of the particular department, which has problems to solve and missions to accomplish, to decide the extent to which science and technology are and can be useful, and can and should be used. I do not think it would serve any useful purpose were the super ministry, of which there has been some mention, to direct other departments of government, such as the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, to lay down a prescription for it or to point out that it is not employing such science, that it is not making enough use of technology, and that more of its resources, for the sake of some principle, should be going into science and technology. More should be going into science and technology if it is useful in accomplishing its main mission. If science and technology are not or cannot be of assistance, there is no sense providing scientists and technologists merely to satisfy some formula or number.
Increasingly it will be the role of the Ministry of Science and Technology to see that newly acquired knowledge is available, that these departments of government have access to this new knowledge in the search for the accomplishment of the most effective way of achieving their particular departmental missions.
In addition to helping out in the application of science and technology for the solution of problems, particularly social problems, in the federal government, I think perhaps the government, particularly my ministry, has a duty and a responsibility to endeavour to see that the same kind of assistance is given to the manufacturing industry.
If I might just be permitted a minute, in Canada we have a rather unique situation with respect to industry in that we have greater, easier, and cheaper access to the largest and most prolific source of science and technology in the world. It is greater than any other country in either the northern or southern hemisphere. The source is the United States, and its neighbour, Canada, enjoys a favourable relationship which no other country enjoys. In some ways we have been fortunate-in many ways in economic terms-in having been granted this ready, easy, and cheap access to technology. It has meant that Canada, unlike a number of other countries in the world, has not had to develop its own science and technology. We have been able to get it easily and cheaply, and consequently we have not engaged in the harder, longer, and more expensive process of developing it for ourselves.
While this has meant that in order to progress economically the cost to us may well have been less, we are vulnerable to the possibility that for one reason or another this source might dry up, and we would then be unprotected and lacking in scientific and technology generating self-sufficiency. Perhaps I should say that this, however, has meant that the investment by Canadian industry in research and development has, for economic reasons, been lower and less than in most other comparably industrialized countries. As I say, this has been cheaper, but it has made us more vulnerable. Recognizing this, the government has instituted a number of programs, mostly in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, designed to reduce this vulnerability and to get a greater level of

May 13, 1976
Science Policy
inherent, indigenous research and development capacity in Canadian industry itself.
With respect to some firms these programs have been very successful indeed, but so far the average has been very low. As a consequence of failure to increase our own capability and to reduce our vulnerability, we as a government are now currently in the process of reviewing the various incentive programs designed to enhance our industrial research and development capability. I hope that during the course of this year a number of these studies will come to fruition, and perhaps we will be able to devise more attractive and more successful incentive programs than those which we have now. These programs and policies have been working to some degree, but not really to the degree that would achieve the kind of progress that seems to be desirable if indeed we want a reasonable measure of invulnerability.
In order to enhance our industrial capability in research and development we have been placing emphasis on what is known as the "make or buy" policy, under which all new research and development projects will be contracted out to the manufacturing industry in Canada in preference to being performed in government laboratories. The test is whether it can be performed outside. It is only in the event it cannot be done in the Canadian manufacturing industry that it becomes a project in a government laboratory, if such capability exists. This means that during this period the laboratory capabilities of the federal government will not be growing at the rate and in the rather spectacular way they did during the early and mid sixties. We are trying to turn new research and development in Canada from the government to the manufacturing industries. If industry does not have the capability or cannot create it, the universities are a second choice. It is only as a laboratory or a locus of last resort that a particular program is carried out within government laboratory apparatus.
Even though it is fairly recent, the "make or buy" policy has been achieving a modest but continuous growth. So far it has been limited to new research projects and new research money. In the last couple of years there have not been large sums of new money for research and development so the developments have not been very significant. It is a step in the right direction, however. Hopefully, when the time comes that useful projects can be found and rather large quantities of money can be made available, then more significant emphasis can be given to the "make or buy" program and significant results quickly achieved. By and large the capacity seems to exist in the Canadian manufacturing industry; what is required is an incentive to get it into operation.
I repeat, Mr. Speaker, I am delighted that this debate has been set afoot by the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth. I think he will agree that considerable efforts are being made by the government in the two areas I have mentioned, even in a year of restraint. Perhaps there is not as much progress as he would like nor is there as much as you and I would like, Mr. Speaker. Given the fact that it is a year of restraint, however, we have to limit our efforts to shifting resources rather than finding new ones. We will continue the endeavours to find better and more effective ways of deploying our available resources in science and
[Mr. Drury.)
technology, but perhaps we will have to wait for a period of more rapid growth in order to take full advantage of what I hope will be new and rather more attractive incentives.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in closing this debate on the motion criticizing the government for its lack of drive in the field of science and technology I think my remarks will dovetail very closely with those just completed by the minister.
This is not a new subject for me. I recall some 18 years ago the same questions coming to the minds of the government led by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). I recall that the issue was basically the same as it is now, that our lack of "go ahead" in the field of science and technology comes down to one word-finance.
When you study what various industrial nations have spent in the field of basic scientific research you will find that Canada ranks as high as any other industrial nation in the world, if you just measure the contribution of govern-
May 13, 1976

ment. The minister implied that tonight in his remarks. When you move on and examine the contribution of the private sector in the field of science and technology, and particularly the application of it, you will find that Canada is lagging seriously. The reason for this lag is obvious; we are a branch plant economy and it is easier to borrow or earn this technology from the parent companies of the branch plants in Canada. Having said all this and heard the minister, I say there is no excuse for this situation to continue indefinitely.
Let me repeat in a general way what has happened under the last two or three governments. In the Diefenbaker government we felt we should encourage private enterprise to move more vigorously into the field of applied technology based on university and government research. We thought we could do it with a system of tax incentives, whereby business could write off 150 per cent of money spent on research. I have looked at the figures and noted what has happened since those days. Our measures had some effect, although small. As the minister said, as companies in Canada could obtain cheaply research information from head offices, branches of multinational corporations operating in Canada did not have much incentive to put money into research in Canada.
I recall this question being debated several times in the early years of the Pearson government, they thought the answer was the establishment of a new department. They took the political science approach and put civil servants in charge of science and technology. They thought that putting a minister at the head of the department would lead us to the promised land and result in greater scientific and technological development. Tonight we heard the minister in charge of that department confess things have moved pretty slowly.
We are examining what is happening in universities and will study how we can improve the relationship between the demand factor for certain disciplines and the supply factor. This is good. Nobody quarrels with this. As well, we could consider what is happening in applied research in Canada. There is no question about this being necessary. I do not think anybody will quarrel with me when I say that Canadian scientists, whether at the university level or working at the government level in Canada, are as good as those of any nation. Our track record with regard to basic science is as good as that of any industrial nation. Our weakness, as the minister suggested, is that we have failed to apply basic science to our problems, the excuse being that we live in a branch plant economy.
This evening I shall not address my remarks to the minister, whom I hold innocent in this matter. I shall talk about the basic problem confronting us, and I return once more to the matter of financing. Every time there is a cry of alarm in this country, every time the nitwits in the Department of Finance say we are moving too quickly, that we need restraint and restriction, the first item on which we cut spending is research. This happens every time. Why? First scientists have no strong political voice to speak for them. Second, they are most vulnerable.
When I became a minister in 1957, I found that the maximum salary for scientists, some of whom had Ph.D.s
Science Policy
and had served the government for 20 years, was in the region of $8,700. At the same time the administrative people, who are always coming to Treasury Board and asking for more, were earning salaries up to the $20,000 level. Mr. Speaker, I sat on that Treasury Board and resisted every effort to increase the salaries of civil servants in Ottawa until the salaries of scientists had been raised. That effort on my part met with some success; at least scientists in the government service today are better paid.
When I was a minister-I suspect it is the same today-I recall seeing all this scientific information for which we had spent a great deal of money piling up and being stored in our libraries. We stored more knowledge than we needed for the next 50 years, knowledge which could apply to almost every field. But there was no awareness of the existence of that knowledge, and it was not put into the hands of the people who needed it. I suppose the classic example is knowledge concerning agriculture, which was stored in the Neatby building. That knowledge was not put into the hands of the public. The reason, again, was the myth that education was a matter for the provinces, and that therefore we must not do anything to give this knowledge, made available to government by the government service and universities, to the people who needed it. That is still going on today.
There is still no federal government service to disseminate or carry abroad knowledge gathered by the National Research Council, the Medical Council, by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, formerly known as mines and technical surveys, by researchers working in the Department of Agriculture, and so on.
Let me also mention forestry. For 20 years our forestry scientists have been advocating the use of knowledge they had gathered for the last 100 years, yet I do not know of a single provincial government using it. Knowledge concerning one of our greatest renewable resources is not being utilized due to the myth that because certain of these services are considered as educational services, the federal government should not touch them. I have spoken on this subject several times in the House in the last ten or 12 years but have seen no change in attitude.
I now come to the present Trudeau administration. I am aware of the government's tax changes, and of write-offs allowed for research. The government allows 150 per cent; yet, I suspect that, as in the days of the Diefenbaker government, that measure has not had much effect. I am thinking of what can be done. I do not say I have all the answers. I suspect that as our capital needs in the next 25 years could amount to several hundreds of millions of dollars, we shall need to invest tremendously in technology and science, so that we may take advantage of technological advances. Technology will be the key. Therefore we are not thinking merely in terms of educating farmers or men in the forestry field.
In future we shall spend huge sums of capital in Canada. Our very survival will be at stake unless we have reasonable access to adequate supplies of energy. We must do all we can to use our basic knowledge and reduce development costs.
Several members of the House have spoken of the farce being played out in areas such as the development of our tar sands. Here we have the government of Ontario, the
13508

May 13, 1976
Science Policy
government of Alberta, and the federal government joining with business in a $2 billion venture to build one Syncrude plant. We are to use our resources to produce oil from the oil sands which will cost us $11 a barrel and up. I suggest that we know that there are two or three other techniques available. One has been available for 20 years, but not mentioned. In this connection I suggest that we must provide incentives. I think we must attack on two fronts. First, we must let the people of Canada know why no government has ever mentioned the other techniques available for the development of the oil sands. I know what they are, and I know why governments are afraid of the technique I have in mind. The reason, of course, has to do with the myth to which I previously referred. That myth must be exposed for the sham it is.
The second approach must be in the field of finance. As the House knows, I put my ideas forward in 1974 to the then minister of finance, and to some other ministers in 1975. And I am pleased to note what is happening.
The headline to an article appearing in the Globe and Mail of May 13, 1976, reads, "175% Recovery Share in Oilfields Proposed Before Big Tax Take." I am interested in the coming announcement. According to the newspaper story, the government next week will make an announcement concerning northern and off-shore oil and gas fields. The government is to give the companies in that field a tax break. It will pledge that, to compensate for risk, the returns from operations will not be milked until the companies have got all their capital back. The government will allow 100 per cent of their capital return, plus 75 per cent to pay for the interest and other costs which they have. After that, the government is really going to hit them.
I am pleased that the government is going to make that announcement because it gets at the basic problem of these capital intensive enterprises. Nearly all these new developments demanding this new science and technology are capital intensive. This gets at the basic cost. Seventy-five per cent of the cost of a modern capital intensive industry goes to the payment of interest. We can no longer avoid that if we continue with out of date techniques of financing.
In the proposals I have made in the past two or three years, one of them, the second choice actually, was this type of proposal. I praised the British government, socialist as it is, for having pioneered this technique in financing.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext: Which government?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO DEVELOP STRONG SCIENCE POLICY
speechtext:
The government of the United Kingdom. It pioneered this type of approach and it looks like our Canadian government is going to apply it. I suggest that in the field of science and technology, if you are going to get small or large Canadian companies to take up the slack which exists in technology, it will have to be by this same type of approach. The government will have to consider that the 150 per cent write-off is not enough. Even the accelerated write-off is not enough.
We will have to go into joint enterprise with these companies whereby we take a part of the risk for them, 10 or 15 per cent, and see that the knowledge that we have

from our government and university circles is put into practical application. The reward that they get will be market return and interest return before we apply any tax to them. However, we, the people, will own shares in those companies and will share in the profits that they make.
I make that point because in my work I have quite a bit to do with newly developing countries around the world. I know the desperate hunger there is for new technology. I know that we in Canada have quite a bit of it, and how saleable it is. However, in many cases our companies are indoctrinated with the concept that you must only move very cautiously and safely, and that if they take the plunge in selling this technology to a foreign country they will be left exposed in case it comes up a bummer.
I suggest that the joint enterprise concept should be extended into foreign countries, particularly the newly developing countries where you take a risk. I can give examples of what I am talking about.
I hope the House will not laugh at this, but recently there was a discovery made by a group of farmers. You take biomass in the form of animal waste and, with a simple physical and chemical action, change it into pure food suitable for recycling through animals. If I talk in dollars qnd cents, what I am talking about becomes more apparent.
If you take a ton of animal waste and use it for fertilizing the land, it is probably worth $2.50 or $3 a ton. If you take that animal waste, remove the methane, that animal waste is probably worth about $30 a ton. If you take that animal waste and put it into pure food suitable for recycling through animals, it is worth $140 a ton. There is the technology discovered by accident by a group of farmers. However, when you go to the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and suggest that they join with a Canadian company, put that technology to work here, and then take it around the world, they say that under their program they are not allowed to do that. They can only support technology that starts and ends in Canada.
The minister should be supported in his statements that we have to take a new look at the programs and new incentives that we have. Thereby, with regard to this motion we are debating today, for nearly two decades we have talked about the necessity of improving our work on science and technology that we are doing on behalf of the Canadian people. Always it is talk. It is time that we took the method into our hands, and went forward and did something in the applied field.
There is no need talking to the House about this being a year of restraint, because the minute you stop scientific development you are carrying out an inflationary policy. The only way you can keep inflation down is to get at your productivity, and 80 to 90 percent of productivity comes from technology. If you are going to keep inflation down, you do not do that by stopping the development of technology in Canada.
I wish the minister would carry this message to his colleagues in cabinet, particularly to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien). Cut out this nonsense by these ministers who simply say to reduce everything 20 per cent, without any awareness of the fact that by reducing the money spent on science and technology they are adding
May 13, 1976

an inflationary force to the country's economy. That is the basic point I wanted to make.
It is not the minister who should be attacked. It should be Treasury Board which works on a pure percentage basis. If the order comes through from the nitwits in Finance that you need to have restraint, the first target they aim at is research into all forms of science and technology. These people have borne the brunt of cuts and slashes every time in the past 15 years.
This motion is well put and timely. It brings to the attention of the Canadian people this phony effort to introduce a program to fight inflation called the AntiInflation Board, which does not even begin to get at the basic causes of inflation. It pretends that it does, and uses that excuse to cut down on research into basic science and technology. That type of attitude on the part of Treasury Board and the government is not serving the country in fighting inflation. In fact it adds to it. I strongly support this motion that the government should really take a hard look at itself, and not use science and technology as the guinea pig in carrying out any form of pretending that they are cutting expenses.
