subtopic: PENSIONS-DENIAL OF PENSION INCREASES TO RETIRED MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES AND RCMP UNTIL AGE 60-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO RECTIFY
PENSIONS-DENIAL OF PENSION INCREASES TO RETIRED MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES AND RCMP UNTIL AGE 60-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO RECTIFY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before three o'clock this afternoon, during the question period, I put a question to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) regarding one aspect of the operations that take place under the Supplementary Retirements Benefits Act.
Usually, as private members, when we put down a question for the late show, we like to have the minister here. I hope I am not expressing anything that the minister will take as a slight when I say I am just as happy to have the parliamentary secretary tonight because, in all honesty, I think he has been connected with this question for a very much longer period. His representation in this House from time to time, in and out, in and out, has been on behalf of a constituency in which a great many public servants reside. He has therefore been obliged to pay some attention to the pensions of public servants.
Adjournment Debate
The question I asked this afternoon had to do with the fact that the escalation of pensions which are paid by the government does not normally begin until the age of 60. I say "normally", because that is not an absolute rule; there are cases of public servants and others whose pensions are escalated prior to age 60, particularly if they are 55 and have put in 30 years of service, or met certain other conditions. But there is the particular case of retired RCMP personnel and retired Canadian armed forces personnel; there are other cases but these are the two main bodies in connection with which this question arises.
Because of their work, the personnel I have mentioned are permitted to retire early. In fact although I say they are permitted, they are, in many cases, forced to retire early. So their pensions begin at an early age. There are some instances of pensions actually beginning in the late forties, though I suppose the more common time for them to begin is in the fifties. Yet despite the fact that most persons who receive government pensions get the escalation once a year in accordance with the rise in the consumer price index, the individuals about whom I am speaking are obliged to wait until they are 60 years of age.
When this measure was first brought in the escalation amounted to only 2 per cent a year and did not mean very much to the persons affected. It was true, also, that at first no civil servants could get the escalation under the age of 60 and it therefore seemed reasonable to deny it to anyone else under 60. But now, when some persons are getting it under the age of 60 and when indexing is in the order of 8, 10 or 11 per cent, the question is of greater importance.
The parliamentary secretary will agree that we had a good discussion on this subject, that we were closest to coming to grips with it during the time when the Special Joint Committee on Employee-Employer Relations in the Public Service dealt with Bill C-52. That was last December. We had before us such persons as Mr. D. N. Nadon, President of the Canadian Forces Long Service Pensioners Association, and Mr. Fred Whitehouse, National Secretary of the Federal Superannuates National Association. Both these men and those associated with them pressed us on this point, and the hon. gentleman knows that somehow or other the notion got around that the government was going to yield, that there was going to be some change in the formula generally known as the 85 rule-that is not a good name for it, incidentally, because not every combination which adds up to 85 does the trick. However, when the crunch came we did not get it, and the people these organizations represent were disappointed.
That was the reason for my question this afternoon to the President of Treasury Board. I reminded him of what happened in December and I dared to hope that maybe by now the matter was being reconsidered. But the answer was no. When I suggested that it be made effective in January, at the time the escalation takes place, at least I had to give him credit for a straightforward answer. He said "no". I found this extremely disappointing, especially after the recognition I thought we had at the committee last December that there was a real case.
I am sure my friend, the parliamentary secretary personally supports the case, but since his minister this afternoon said no he cannot stand up tonight and say yes. However, I

hope he will tell me, as one who is close to the throne that he will go to bat and try to persuade his minister that this issue we thought we had resolved last December does need to be considered again, and that action should be taken on it just as soon as possible.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: PENSIONS-DENIAL OF PENSION INCREASES TO RETIRED MEMBERS OF ARMED FORCES AND RCMP UNTIL AGE 60-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO RECTIFY
speechtext:
Various combination will arrive at it. They start age 59 if they have 26 years service, at age 58 with 27 years service, and so on to age 55 for a member with 30 or more years service.
This formula was determined after consultation with representatives of the Canadian forces and the RCMP, bearing in mind the amendments made in 1971 to the Public Service Superannuation Act which permitted public servants to retire on full accrued pensions at age 55 if they had over 30 years service. Such pensions were subject to yearly increases under the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act. In order to correct this anomaly between Public Service employees and members of other groups, the formula mentioned above was established with retroactive effect to January 1, 1973. However, it was felt that any further lowering of the age at which retired members of the Canadian forces or the RCMP could receive pension increases would have created a different anomaly in comparison with pensions under the Public Service Superannuation Act.
Under the forces pension plan, and others, individuals can retire at a much earlier age than public servants and receive their full pension. Therefore it was considered equitable to begin payment of pension increases to retired forces members at the same age at which long service public servants can receive both their full pension and the escalation.
Further, in looking at what the needs of retired members of the forces, public service and others may be, it seemed reasonable to expect that those who retire at younger ages are more likely to be able to find alternative employment. In such instances, the need for earlier escalation of pensions did not seem so acute as for those who have reached age 60, or over age 55 with long service, and who are more likely to have retired from active working life.
As my hon. friend mentioned, during the consideration of the Statute Law (Superannuation) Amendment Act by the Standing Committee of the House of Commons and the Senate on Employer-Employee Relations in the Public Service, the suggestion was made for a change in the escalation formula for members of the armed forces and the RCMP and these were considered. However, the govern-

ment could not see its way clear at that time or indeed, at present, to introduce such an amendment.
I can assure the hon. member that, in the on-going review of pension legislation, consideration will continue to be given to this matter although at present the government has no plans to introduce such an amendment for January of next year.

subtopic: MANPOWER-MEASURES TO PROVIDE EMPLOYMENT FOR STUDENTS
MANPOWER-MEASURES TO PROVIDE EMPLOYMENT FOR STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I debate the issue tonight of student unemployment because of the precarious position with which we will be faced in Canada this summer as students graduate or return from universities to face a summer of almost record unemployment in Canadian history.
In my question to the minister yesterday I indicated that the total thrust of the summer student employment program would produce only some 12,000 jobs from 17 programs, and this will be only about 1.2 per cent of those seeking work. With a student population of some one million this will only be an insignificant dent in the need.
I recognize that, as the minister said in reply, I chose to refer only to programs of direct job creation. Indeed that is what we are looking for, direct job creation. He also said that the main effort of the government, and the one offering the greatest degree of success, is the increased co-operation of the private sector in placing students this summer. However, I fail to understand what this will achieve when we have an unemployment rate of 7.4 per cent.
As much as I want to be fair, I fail to see how the government will create 109,000 unpaid activities for students and summer jobs for an anticipated 200,000 students as a result of the national "Hire a Student" campaign. All I can say is that the government can come out with fancy names for programs which are varied and many, but cannot produce jobs.
The minister also in his reply evaded my request that he make a statement on motions to declare the programs which would realistically combat youth unemployment. He answered to the effect that all members were aware of the many and varied programs which were available. Well, I am aware of each and every program that was announced. I will list some of them. They include the Summer '76 program, the Information and Evaluation Program, the Summer Puppet Program, health activities, student community services, cadet training, community assistance, reserve training, parks awareness, Parks Canada, native employment, and many other programs to stimulate employment as the minister indicated.
I know about these programs, Mr. Speaker. I must know about them because of the embarrassing rate of unemployment in my district of Newfoundland. I also know that I will be getting hundreds of letters from students and parents of students wondering why there are no jobs available. The parents will be asking how their sons are to go
May 13, 1976

back to university, or indeed enter university, and the students will be asking the same thing. I will be receiving letters from high school graduates who will want a job so that they can earn enough money to enter university because some politician told him or her on their graduation about the wonderful world of opportunity we have in Canada.
I will also be receiving letters from university graduates who were told the value of a university degree. They will not be able to find that golden horizon they have been told about. I also know what the facts are. The facts are that for the 14 to 24 age group the unemployment rate for March, 1976, was 14.8 per cent for males, 11.5 per cent for females, an average of some 13 per cent. As of this date 348,000 in this age group are unemployed. This constitutes 45.8 per cent of the entire unemployed population of Canada and yet this age group only accounts for 26.4 per cent of the population.
Based on Statistics Canada figures, student unemployment peaks in June and gradually dwindles by August. In
1975	the labour force figures were 839,000 in June, 1,000,043 in July, and 984,000 in August. So, even if the minister's figures by any stretch of the imagination are correct, this will prove to be a critical summer for student employment. Yet the government has cancelled the OFY program, and the LIP program has been cut back. While LIP does not sponsor students directly it has been a source of student employment in the past.
I know that I will get the answer that OFY was cancelled because of restraints, but this is hypocritical because students will have to make excessive demands on student loan programs or there will be an additional burden on the over-burdened Unemployment Insurance Commission fund, increased social welfare payments, let alone the social spill-over.
We need only refer to the report of the committee on youth which, when referring to the high level of youth unemployment, said this:
The present tragedy is more than personal; it is societal in scope. Canadian society cannot cease to generate a broad range of options for its youth in the employment field.
I hope that the government realizes what a burdensome problem youth unemployment will be this summer, but it will not be overcome by expensive and meaningless ads that shout slogans such as "Have a Young Summer", or asking business and industry to "Hire a Student," when each day, almost repeatedly, there are more and more lay-offs in business and industry.
The government must initiate a massive youth employment program immediately. I do not see how it can avoid doing so. I hope that the reply I receive tonight will offer some hope of plans by the government to alleviate serious student unemployment which threatens our youth in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Fleming (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: MANPOWER-MEASURES TO PROVIDE EMPLOYMENT FOR STUDENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the summer of
1976	an estimated 85 per cent of an anticipated student labour force of 1.3 million will find work in the private sector. Therefore to communicate the student hiring philosophy to employers across Canada, the Department of Manpower and Immigration is presently engaged in an
Adjournment Debate
intensive hire-a-student advertising campaign. They have been joined in this effort by the five major banks in Canada which will display their promotional material in some 6,000 branch offices across Canada. The message urges employers to hire students either for the entire summer or on a casual basis. This program is increased in size over previous years, but with no increase in costs. This has been accomplished by repeating last year's program, thus allowing savings to be channeled into a media campaign that will permit a wider distribution of publicity material.
In addition, the minister has personally written to all his provincial counterparts to request that every effort be made, despite present fiscal restraints, to create as many summer employment opportunities as possible. It is expected that provincial governments across Canada will spend approximately $48 million and create 60,000 jobs.
The federal effort will be in two areas. The first is the student summer employment and activities program in which eight federal departments operate 17 individual programs and create opportunities for an additional 109,000 to participate in unpaid activities, and includes some 300 Canada Manpower Centres for students which will operate across Canada in 1976, and it is anticipated that some
200,000	students will be placed in employment through these centres. The second is direct departmental hiring in which federal departments hire large numbers of students to supplement regular staff on holidays or increase regular departmental activities during the summer period. However, as these funds are within regular resources available to departments, it is difficult to calculate the total expenditures. Estimates provided by departments in September, 1975, for 1976 indicated that some 10,000 jobs would be created, costing individual departments approximately $17 million.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to raise a question tonight in the adjournment debate with respect to a matter which I raised some time ago in the question period with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) relating to the re-appointment of a minister responsible for multiculturalism. The fact of the matter is that the Prime Minister at that time indicated to me in a rather extended reply that he and the government had no interest in the appointment of a minister for this portfolio.
We all know that prior to the last election this portfolio was occupied by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Hai-dasz). He was in fact given a great deal of profile with respect to the interest of the government regarding the third force in this country. I think it is interesting to remind ourselves in the House that fully one third of our population in Canada is neither of French nor English extraction. I suggest it represents a very important force in our country, one that requires reasonable representation within cabinet. I am sorry to say that the condideration that this group has so far received has been a consistent and continuing downgrading of multicultural concerns in our country.

May 13, 1976
Adjournment Debate
In the brief time I have at my disposal I should like to refer to what I think is a very appropriate and telling editoral from the Toronto Globe and Mail. I think this editorial really puts the finger on the matter of the multicultural program-or the lack of it-of the government. This editorial appeared on December 1, 1975, and in part it stated:
The multicultural program which Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau draped noisily upon his government's shoulders in 1971, was-to pick the best words for it-intended solely to persuade those Canadians of other than French and English mother tongues that they would not be neglected while Ottawa pushed ahead with official biculturalism and bilingualism. In short, a bribe-to buy off opponents of bi-and-bi-and a bribe of rather cynical dimensions.
The game plan was to pick a Polish-Canadian from the Liberal caucus, Dr. Stanley Haidasz, give him a cabinet title of Minister of State for Multiculturalism and let him have millions of dollars to hand out for ethnic poetry readings and choir singing and costumed dances and similar forms of ancestral consciousness-raising and-in particular-government advertising in the ethnic press.
All that, however, is the past. There is a new game plan (multiculturalism lost its Minister of State some time ago and shrank into a branch office of the Minister of Labour). We hear now from Labour Minister John Munro that the "folkloric aspects" of multiculturalism are going to be de-emphasized and instead there is going to be something called "group understanding" and "combatting discrimination"-all, mind you, at no extra cost.
Meaning?
We frankly have no idea and we doubt if anyone in the country does. Mr. Munro gives no specifics, no details, not even hints-except to coyly reveal that it will include government measures that are, or should be, already in place, such as Justice Department action against discrimination. So does National Health and Welfare next announce that it is changing its policies to support motherhood?
The government cannot be honest enough to say that what it is trying to do is pare its spending. (And, indeed, multiculturalism's budget has shrunk to about half of what it had in the halycon Haidasz days.) But we have our doubts about whether the government will do anything to save money and we suspect that the sum product of Mr. Munro's new policy will be to insult ethnic minorities with its emptiness.
As I pointed out, about one third of our population is of neither French nor English extraction, but if we compare the amount of money which is expended with respect to that portion we will see that there is in excess of $350 million for the biculturalism and bilingualism program as opposed to something like $7 million for the multiculturalism program.
Quite frankly, one is not surprised at the lack of representation of people from other than French and English extraction on the government side. There is very small representation from the third force of this country, and I suggest that the reason is that the government has no interest, except at election time, in giving anything but lip service to multiculturalism. It is an insult to that third of our population. The fact of the matter is that people in our society, such as my colleagues, the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski), the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall), and other people in our party, are members of this third portion of our country. We all try to speak out and to encourage the government to do something tangible to encourage the
ethnic traditions we and our forefathers have brought to this country, but I am afraid it all falls on deaf ears.
It was a specious argument the Prime Minister gave to me when he answered my question and tried to relate multiculturalism to the fact that he did not want to create other portfolios and expand the cabinet to unreasonable proportions. The fact is, that we had a portfolio of multiculturalism. The government is only playing a political game. I can assure the parliamentary secretary who is here to answer on behalf of the minister that the one third of the population which falls in this category will not be fooled in the next election. They will look back at the record of the government, and I can assure the hon. parliamentary secretary that the government may expect that one third of Canada's population will make their feelings known.

speakeroldname: Mr. Fernand E. Leblanc (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) for his recent appointment by his new leader. I am convinced that this is an acknowledgment of his constant and excellent work.
The question raised tonight has already been answered several times before. In particular, on November 26, 1975, as show on page 9457 of the French Hansard, the Prime Minister indicated his difficulties in organizing his cabinet so as not to exceed the number required to serve the Canadian people well. He mentioned that there were many areas where the appointment of a minister would be useful. Moreover, he said the following:
... the government does not intend to lend any less emphasis to its strong belief in the policy on multiculturalism.
In fact, the last budget shows this since no cuts were made in this program. To administer the program, the minister responsible has a vast experience within the cabinet, of which he has been a member since 1968, after having been parliamentary secretary, and, like myself, all Canadians recognize his devotion and his great involvement in multiculturalism.
Like the President of the Treasury Board, I am convinced that the opposition should make up its mind either to accept willingly budgetary increases or to stop to continually urge the government to increase all its budgetary items.
I would also like to mention that the Minister of Labour has not announced any fundamental change in the multiculturalism program. In fact, he announced his intention to evaluate the result of this program, which is only five years old, and perhaps to reallocate funds so as to insist on certain aspects which seem to have been neglected.
However, Mr. Speaker, you can be assured that I would be proud and happy to accept the position recommended by my hon. friend if the Prime Minister judged it appropriate and if the budget allowed it.
